The pipeline processes six input images from a patient, outputting the probability for a single task in single-task mode or for all tasks in multi-task mode. 4. Method 4.1. Data Preprocessing 4.1.1. Stain Normalization In examining the effect of stain inconsistency on diagnostic and prognostic tasks within our dataset, we apply three well-established stain normalization techniques: Reinhard , Vahadane , and Macenko . For each image in the training set, a random image from the same set is chosen as a reference, and the corresponding stain normalization method is used to align the stain profile of the original image with that of the target. This approach results in four distinct training datasets: the original dataset and three versions augmented by different normalization methods. The final performance is evaluated on each dataset, allowing us to analyze the impact of various stain normalization techniques on generalization across different stain variations. 4.1.2. Images Transform Several data augmentation techniques are implemented during model training to enhance the diversity and robustness of the training data. Due to the large size of the original images, we resize all images to 512 × 512 pixels. For data augmentation, we always apply z-score normalization, random cropping, and random rotation, while other techniques such as contrast adjustment, sharpness adjustment, horizontal/vertical flipping, and contrast adjustments are applied with a 50% probability. For the validation and test sets, normalization alone is applied to maintain consistency in evaluation. Furthermore, the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE)  is used to address class imbalance, generating synthetic samples for underrepresented classes. 4.2. Model Architecture Compared to other microscope image datasets, the challenges in our Multi-OSCC dataset include fusing features from multiple images at varying magnifications and handling multiple tasks. To address these, we design a network architecture for multi-image feature fusion, enabling flexible integration of pre-trained models, feature fusion modules, and multi-task learning optimization algorithms. The architecture of our network is shown in Figure 2. 4.2.1. Vision Backbone We explore several popular vision models in recent years, including Res Net , Dense Net , Vision Transformer (Vi T) , and Swin Transformer V2 (Swin) . These models include both CNN and Transformer architectures. 1. Res Net50 utilizes residual learning through skip connections, containing 50 convolutional layers grouped into residual blocks. 2. Dense Net121 comprises multiple dense blocks, where each layer is directly connected to all subsequent layers through dense connectivity. 3. Vi T-Base/Small: Transformer-based models that treat image patches as tokens and leverage self-attention for image classification. Both Vi T-Base and Vi T-Small have 12 layers, but Vi T-Small features a smaller embedding size compared to Vi T-Base. 4. Swin-Base utilizes hierarchical Transformer structures with shifted-window attention mechanisms for efficient vision tasks. We used the base model which has 24 layers and outputs embeddings of size 1024. Jinquan Guan, et al.: Preprint submitted to Elsevier Page 5 of 12 Instead of training the models from scratch, we use transfer learning by loading pre-trained models from existing work and fine-tuning the backbone models with end-toend training. We test seven different backbones, including Res Net50, Dense Net121, Vi T-Base, and Swin-Base with Image Net  pre-trained weights, Vi T-Small with Patho Bench  weights, and Vi TBase with weights from Hibou  and CONCH . We utilize the Image Net pretrained model from the timm library. The detailed pathological pre-trained models are described below. 1. Pahto Bench: It utilized the DINO  pre-training method to train a Vi T-Small model, leveraging a dataset comprising 32.6 million patches from various cancers, all stained with H&E at two different magnification levels ×20 and ×40. 2. CONCH: It employs a visual-language model with the Vi T-Base architecture as the image encoder. The image encoder is first pre-trained with the i BOT  method on a dataset of 16 million image patches, covering over 350 cancer subtypes. It is then fine-tuned on a dataset of more than 1.17 million image-caption pairs. The image encoder from the CONCH model serves as the pre-trained weights for this process. 3. Hibou-B: The Hibou-B model is pre-trained using 512 million clean patches with the DINOv2  pre-training method. The dataset consisted of H&E and non-H&E stained slides, human tissues, veterinary biopsies, and is enriched with cytology slides. 4.2.2. Feature Fusion Module We experiment with four different feature fusion modules: Concatenation, Low-rank Multimodal Fusion (LMF) , Gated Fusion, and Transformer. These modules are designed to merge multiple features into a single representation to help with the subsequent classification tasks. Concatenation simply combines the features from different images. The LMF method, which builds on Tensor Fusion, enhances computational efficiency by parallelizing the decomposition of tensors and weights using low-rank factors specific to each modality. The Gated Fusion method employs a gating mechanism to regulate the flow of information between features. In our implementation of the gating mechanism, we assume the features of each image are represented as 𝑒𝑖. The process is as follows: 𝑒𝑖is passed through a sigmoid function to obtain 𝑎𝑖, and through a tanh function to produce 𝑡𝑖. The final output is computed as 𝑍= ∑5 𝑖=0(𝑒𝑖⋅𝑡𝑖). The Transformer method in this research employs a 2-layer Transformer encoder  to facilitate information interaction among six feature vectors extracted from six images. This approach ultimately aggregates multiview representations by computing the mean of enhanced feature embeddings derived from the six images. These modules are placed after the shared vision backbone to fuse the features extracted from six images of a patient. 4.2.3. Classic multi-task learning models are generally categorized into three types: hard parameter sharing, soft parameter sharing, or a combination of both . In our study, we employ the hard parameter sharing approach due to its efficiency and fewer parameter requirements.Specifically, we evaluate three different multi-task learning algorithms: Sum Loss, Grad Norm , and Pareto . The Sum Loss method directly sums the loss of all tasks, while Grad Norm dynamically balances the gradient magnitudes across tasks to balance adaptive loss. The Pareto method optimizes multiple objectives by finding solutions that are not dominated by any other, to achieve the pareto optimality. These algorithms are used to optimize the shared and task-specific parameters in our model. 4.2.4. Classification Head For each task, we use a standard multi-layer perceptron (MLP) as the classification head. This MLP architecture includes five layers in total, with four hidden layers sized at 768, 256, 128, and 64 units and a classification layer sized at 2 units. After each hidden layer, we employ the rectified linear unit (Re LU) activation function  and layer normalization (Layer Norm)  to enhance the stability and convergence of the model. To mitigate overfitting, we also apply a dropout  with a probability of 0.5 following the final hidden layer, preceding the output layer that maps to the number of classes. 5. Discussion In this section, we discuss in more detail the characteristics of our proposed dataset and its value for future research. Our dataset provides labels for multiple targets, supporting a wide range of studies, including multi-task learning and the development of more generalizable models. In our analysis, the highest AUC for the REC task reached 94.72%, and the highest AUC for the TD task is 81.23%. Additionally, the optimal AUC for other tasks exceeded 70%, demonstrating histopathology images’ effectiveness in prognostic predictions and cancer differentiation diagnosis, and enabling research across broader diagnostic applications. Our data collection methodology aligns with approaches outlined by Chaudhary et al.  and Rahman et al. , where histopathology images are captured using a microscope at various high magnifications. We opted for electronic microscopy over WSI for collecting these histopathology images. As detailed in Section 3, electronic microscopy is a simpler technique. Previous work, such as Lu et al. , has explored alternative methods for acquiring pathological images (e.g., using mobile phones), which makes this data collection approach feasible in resourceconstrained environments. This also addresses the challenge of large data volumes in pathological image analysis from a resolution perspective, as representative regions can be effectively sampled from histopathology images . We acknowledge that relying solely on electronic microscopy, compared to WSI, might lead to some information loss. To mitigate this, we captured images at multiple resolutions and from various lesion locations to preserve more comprehensive information. The high AUC achieved in our benchmark results (Section 5.9) and the multi-site analysis (Section 5.4) collectively demonstrate the efficacy of supplementing representative histopathology images, thereby validating the feasibility of our data collection method. Therefore, from both a technical standpoint and an analysis of experimental metrics, this dataset possesses significant clinical utility and offers a valuable reference for future work. In clinical practice, prognosis and diagnosis are closely linked and often exhibit positive correlations; an experienced clinician typically considers multiple aspects concurrently . Modeling a single task tends to overlook the interdependencies among various diagnostic and prognostic factors, making it imperative to incorporate multiple objectives into the modeling process. We have explored classical multi-task learning approaches in experiments. However, performance tends to decline when tasks are learned simultaneously, underscoring the need for more effective multi-task learning algorithms and a more powerful foundation model. 7. Conclusion This paper introduces Multi-OSCC, a novel clinical scenario-oriented multi-task dataset for OSCC diagnosis and prognosis, accompanied by comprehensive benchmarks under single-task and multi-task settings. Our key findings include: (1) introducing pathology-specific pre-training substantially improves both OSCC diagnosis and prognosis performance; (2) tumor recurrence prediction is highly sensitive to color variations, with stain normalization improving diagnostic tasks but impairing recurrence prediction, highlighting the need for task-specific preprocessing; and (3) while single-task models achieve promising AUC scores, balancing performance across diverse clinical tasks remains challenging for multi-task frameworks, highlighting avenues for future innovation. To encourage further research, we have made the dataset publicly available, paving the way toward improved automated systems for automated clinical evaluation of OSCC. context: Experience is the Best Teacher: Grounding VLMs for Robotics through Self-Generated Memory Guowei Lan1 * Kaixian Qu1 * Ren´e Zurbr¨ugg1 2 Changan Chen1 Christopher E. Mower3 Haitham Bou-Ammar3 4 Marco Hutter1 1Robotic Systems Lab, ETH Zurich 2ETH AI Center 3Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab 4UCL Centre for AI Figure 1: Robot completes a new task guided by previously self-generated memory. We propose grounding VLMs through memory generated by the robot itself from direct hardware experiments, establishing awareness of the robot’s own capability. When executing a novel task, the robot keeps a short-term memory that helps the robot reflect and complete the task (illustrated in the grey clip). The experience is then stored as long-term memory and retrieved to guide the VLM’s task planning whenever a similar scenario is encountered (illustrated in the main figure). Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have been widely adopted in robotics to enable autonomous planning. However, grounding VLMs, originally trained on internet data, to diverse real-world robots remains a challenge. This paper presents EXPTEACH, a framework that grounds VLMs to physical robots by building a self-generated memory of real-world experiences. In EXPTEACH, the VLM autonomously plans actions, verifies outcomes, reflects on failures, and adapts robot behaviors in a closed loop. The self-generated experiences during this process are then summarized into a long-term memory, enabling retrieval of learned knowledge to guide future tasks via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Additionally, EXPTEACH enhances the spatial understanding of VLMs with an on-demand image annotation module. In experiments, we show that reflection improves success rates from 36% to 84% on four challenging robotic tasks and observe the emergence of intelligent object interactions, including creative tool use. Across extensive tests on 12 real-world scenarios (including eight unseen ones), we find that grounding with long-term memory boosts single-trial success rates from 22% to 80%, demonstrating the effectiveness and generalizability of EXPTEACH. Keywords: robot memory, vision-language models, task planning *These authors contributed equally to this work. Correspondence to Kaixian Qu ar Xiv:2507.16713v1 [cs.RO] 22 Jul 2025 1 Introduction Recently, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated near-human performance across a range of reasoning tasks, showcasing emergent capabilities in diverse domains such as mathematics and programming . These broad competencies have enabled LLMs to move beyond traditional language tasks and play an increasingly important role in robotics. In particular, they are now widely used in task planning, where LLMs interpret natural language instructions and generate feasible action plans with common-sense reasoning . To address the limitations of text-only input, research has increasingly shifted toward multimodal models, especially vision-language models (VLMs) that jointly process visual and textual data. Recent VLMs  exhibit strong multimodal reasoning and high-resolution visual processing. Building on these capabilities, recent work has leveraged VLMs to enable robots to reason about visual inputs and develop closed-loop, autonomous systems . This approach reduces reliance on manually designed components such as explicit scene descriptors . However, grounding VLMs, originally trained on internet data, to diverse real-world robots remains a challenge. For example, in the scenario depicted in Figure 1, when seeing a tennis ball partially occluded by a fan, a VLM often confidently instructs the robot to pick up the ball. While this aligns with human intuition–since humans can often act successfully based on partial visibility–robots typically struggle to grasp the ball due to imperfect object perception. This raises a critical question: how can we make the VLM aware of the specific capabilities of the robot it is assisting? How can we effectively ground VLMs for robotics? One promising direction lies in augmenting VLMs with memory, a core brain-based capability underpinning human cognition . Incorporating memory of past experience into LLM agents has shown potential for improving decision-making in complex tasks . In robotics, memory has been used to help agents retain contextual information to support tasks such as navigating familiar environments , and to enable more natural and effective human–robot interaction . Building on these developments, we investigate whether VLMs, when deployed on real robots, can generate their own memory to ground themselves in the specific capabilities and limitations of the robot. This paper presents EXPTEACH, which grounds VLMs for robotics through a self-generated memory of past experiences. The central idea behind EXPTEACH is that, even if initially poorly grounded, a VLM can autonomously complete instructions efficiently and use the resulting selfgenerated experiences to progressively ground itself via a memory mechanism. To realize this, EXPTEACH hinges on three pivotal components: (i) a VLM success detector for autonomous feedback; (ii) a short-term memory (STM) that enables intelligent adaptation; and (iii) a long-term memory (LTM) that stores past experiences. Upon receiving a new instruction, EXPTEACH retrieves relevant experiences from the LTM to ground the VLM through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) . Additionally, EXPTEACH enhances the spatial understanding of VLMs with an on-demand image annotation module. We evaluate our approach on multiple challenging real-world tasks and show that this grounding technique significantly strengthens the robot’s performance. This paper presents the following key contributions: • A self-generated memory framework combining short-term and long-term memory to ground VLMs in robotic planning. • A memory retrieval strategy using RAG to access task-relevant prior experiences from LTM, enabling the robot to act correctly in future tasks with similar instructions and scenes. • An on-demand image annotation module that enhances spatial reasoning across multiple skills, leading to more accurate and robust action execution with VLMs. • Extensive real-world evaluations demonstrating that EXPTEACH significantly improves success rates through both STM and LTM, and generalizes effectively to unseen tasks. 2 2 Related Work VLMs in Robotics. LLMs have demonstrated strong capabilities in robotics . Recent developments in VLMs  have further propelled the field by integrating visual perception into reasoning . Prior research has explored the use of VLMs in various robotics tasks, such as generating action sequences from visual and language inputs , assessing action outcomes and failure recovery . In this work, we build on these approaches by using a VLM as both a task planner and a success detector, enabling closed-loop task execution. Image Annotation for Action Planning. Annotating images is an effective approach to help ground VLMs for precise action planning . Recent works combines object-centric annotations (masks aligned directly with objects) with grasping tools to support more challenging tasks such as semantic object grasping . However, these approaches are typically limited to planar tabletop manipulation or grasping alone. In contrast, EXPTEACH introduces an on-demand image annotation tool that enables grounded actions in 3D space for multiple skills beyond 6-Do F grasping. Self-Reflection and Robot Memory. Recent work has explored ways for LLM-enabled robots to reflect on their failures  and to learn from a diverse range of experiences . However, these systems typically require external supervision signals, as there is no visual feedback from the LLM itself. Recent advances in VLMs have enabled robots to plan, verify, and self-reflect using a single VLM model with raw sensor input . Our approach, EXPTEACH, investigates whether reflection can lead to emergent intelligent object interactions (including tool use) and how such experiences enhance future performance. While aligning with recent work on autonomous memory generation for VLM agents , EXPTEACH specifically focuses on grounding VLMs to robots through real-world experiments. The task planner T , implemented as a pretrained VLM, is responsible for planning a sequence of actions (skill instantiations at = πk(arg)) that fulfill the instruction I. At each timestep t, the planner observes the environment ot through RGB-D input and selects an action at for the robot to execute. In addition, T can leverage contextual information C to guide planning. Our work investigates how the planner T , a VLM originally trained on internet data and unaware of the specific embodiment, can be effectively and efficiently grounded to the robot’s capabilities through this contextual information C. Furthermore, we explore whether such grounding can be achieved autonomously–that is, whether the VLM can generate C on its own by self-correcting its behaviors and using that to ground itself. 3 Figure 2: EXPTEACH pipeline overview. At the start of each task, the system takes the user instruction I and egocentric observation o0, which the VLM summarizes into a scenario. RAG retrieves relevant experiences from long-term memory M (section 4.3) and, together with the instruction and observation, feeds them into the VLM task planner T (section 4.1) to generate the next action a. After execution, success is checked by the VLM. If the task is not completed, the action a and its feedback r are accumulated into short-term memory m (section 4.2) and fed back into planning. Once the task is completed, the short-term memory m is summarized and stored in long-term memory M for future use. 4 Method EXPTEACH leverages the VLM task planner T and success detector D as the core components for closed-loop planning (section 4.1). The VLM task planner T is enhanced with a memory mechanism comprising a short-term memory m (section 4.2), which records actions taken for the current instruction I, and a long-term memory M (section 4.3), which stores past experiences. In addition, the VLM planner T may activate an on-demand image annotation tool to enhance its spatial reasoning capabilities (section 4.4). An overview of the framework is provided in Figure 2. 4.1 VLM Task Planning We use the same VLM for both the task planner T and the success detector D. Both components use the function-calling interface to enforce a structured output format, such as push(object="apple"). The VLM task planner T interprets user instructions I and generates action plans from RGB images. After each action a is executed, the VLM success detector D evaluates the feedback signal r from visual observation o. This feedback includes a scene description, action outcome (success or failure), failure analysis for recovery, and suggestions for the next action. The feedback is then passed to the task planner T via the STM. 4.2 Short-Term Memory Short-term memory m in our framework plays a critical role in grounding VLMs in robots to dynamically reflect, replan, and recover from failures during task execution. As depicted in Figure 2, the short-term memory m operates in an iterative pipeline, interacting closely with the task planner T and success detector D. It stores the generated action log until time t. More precisely, each entry records the action a and its associated feedback r from D, m = {(aτ, rτ+1)}t−1 τ=0 = {(aτ, D(aτ, oτ+1))}t−1 τ=0 (1) In cases of action failure, the short-term memory enables the robot to identify better strategies for achieving the task—for example, interacting with non-target objects to facilitate grasping or using 4 tools to manipulate small objects. STM can significantly improve success rates within the allotted attempts for challenging tasks. 4.3 Long-Term Memory The LTM M plays a pivotal role in grounding VLMs for robotics by autonomously accumulating knowledge and experience over time. Specifically, upon successful completion of a task, the robot’s STM m contents are summarized by a VLM experience summarizer E and stored into the LTM as a key-value pair (K, E) where the key K is the scenario description (which consists of the user instruction I and the initial scene description from the RGB image o0), and the value is the associated summarized experience E, as illustrated in Figure 2. Algorithm 1 EXPTEACH Given: Instruction I, initial obs. o0 Internal: Long-term memory M 1: K′ ←EMBED(I, o0) 2: {(Ki, Ei)}k i=1 ←RAG(K′, M) 3: t ←0, m ←∅ 4: repeat 5: at ←T (I, ot, m, {(Ki, Ei)}k i=1) 6: Execute at and receive ot+1 7: rt+1 ←D(at, ot+1) 8: m ←m ∪(at, rt+1) 9: t ←t + 1 10: until rt.completed 11: M ←M ∪{(K′, E(m))} When presented with a new task, the task planner T retrieves relevant prior experiences E from the LTM M through a RAG process. A new retrieval key (scenario) is formed by combining the current user instruction I and scene description o. This key is embedded into a real-valued vector using Open AI’s text-embedding-3-large model . In the LTM, each stored scenario maintains a cached embedding from the same model. RAG then uses cosine similarity to retrieve the top-k most relevant past experiences E, which are incorporated into the task planning prompt. Through this retrieval and augmentation mechanism, the robot gains access to relevant prior experiences, allowing it to act correctly from the outset. In summary, the LTM grounds VLMs in robotic experience, providing relevant knowledge that enables the robot to plan correctly and even generalize to unseen but similar situations. Algorithm 1 illustrates this process. 4.4 Enhanced Skillset with Image Annotations Pick up drumstick. ✅ ✅ Push grape to banana. Figure 3: Illustration of image annotation tools. We focus on three manipulation skills—pick, place, and push. Identifying a suitable location for each action is non-trivial: purely geometric grasp planning may seize an undesirable part (e.g., the meat on a skewer or the ice-cream top rather than its cone), and effective placing or pushing likewise demands semantic scene understanding. To address these challenges, we introduce an on-demand image-annotation tool that is shared across all skills. Given a user instruction I and the current RGB frame ot, VLM first selects the skill to execute with its parameters (object name, whether image annotation is needed, etc.). The robot then performs open-vocabulary segmentation with Grounded SAM , which integrates Grounding DINO  and SAM , producing an initial object mask. If the VLM requests a second annotation pass, our image overlays a set of candidate location masks on the image, allowing the VLM to choose the most appropriate location for the current action a. Figure 3 illustrates this procedure for the pick and push actions. For placing, we apply farthest-point sampling (FPS)  on the segmented mask to generate candidate placement locations, whereas for pushing, we draw candidate goal masks that denote the end points. In both cases, the VLM evaluates the annotated options and selects the most suitable location, as illustrated in Figure 3. For grasping, the segmented point cloud is first passed to Any Grasp , which returns a set of grasp hypotheses accompanied by confidence scores sconf ∈. Grasp poses that violate kinematic constraints are filtered out through inverse-kinematics checks using 5 Pinocchio , yielding the feasible subset G. If the VLM determines that image annotation is beneficial (typically not the case for simple objects like an apple), our annotation tool similarly performs FPS within the object mask to generate a collection of numbered location masks for the VLM to select from. The final grasp is selected by maximizing the product of two scores: g= arg maxg∈G sconf(g) · sloc(g), (2) where sloc(g) ∈ denotes the location score, computed based on the normalized Euclidean distance between grasp g and the chosen location. 5 Results 5.1 Experiment Setup In our experiments, we use a legged manipulator that combines ANYmal , a quadrupedal robot, with a 6-Do F arm. The arm is equipped with a Robotiq 2F-140 gripper for object manipulation and a ZED X Mini Stereo Camera mounted on the elbow. For the VLM, we employ gpt-4o , with the prompt details provided in the Appendix. If the robot fails an action and alters the environment, a human operator intervenes to reset the scene, after which the robot resumes execution. 5.2 Evaluation of Short-Term Memory and Self-Reflection To evaluate the effectiveness of the STM and reflection module at efficiently generating successful episodes, even after initial failures, we designed a series of challenging object manipulation tasks. For the baseline, we use Ca P-V, which enhances Ca P  by incorporating visual feedback. This baseline does not have STM and selects the next action solely based on the current image and user instruction, without the ability to reflect on failed actions. Experimental results in Table 2 highlight the critical role of STM and reflection in achieving successful task completion. Without STM, the robot tends to repeat the same failures without adapting, leading to poor task performance. Table 2: Effect of STM on success rates. For example, when instructed to “put the apple on the plate,” and faced with a partially obstructing container, the robot initially fails to grasp the apple due to poor perception. After detecting the failure, the VLM decides to push away the container and successfully retries the grasp (see Figure 1). Similarly, when told to “move the candy to the banana,” the robot fails to push the candy with its gripper due to insufficient contact. Upon reflection, the VLM autonomously chooses to use a sponge as a tool to push more effectively (see Figure 4). After cracking an egg while grasping, the VLM similarly learns to push rather than grasp fragile objects. In another case, when asked to “collect the bowl,” the robot initially drops an apple from the bowl during execution because it overlooked the object. After the user intervenes and rebuilds the scene, the robot reflects and modifies its strategy: “I should first move the apple to the table before picking up the bowl” (see Figure 4). Note that this is the only instance where we let a human judge success, as the robot technically picked up the bowl, but the apple dropping was unacceptable and should be treated as a failure. 6 Figure 4: Examples of EXPTEACH on different scenarios. In the first STM example (top row), after failing to push the candy with its gripper, the robot reflects and uses a sponge as a tool. In the second STM example (middle row), after dropping the apple during bowl collection, the robot reflects with user feedback and learns to move the apple first. These experiences are then summarized and stored in the LTM, allowing the robot to generalize its learning to similar future scenarios (bottom row). For example, when asked to “Move the screw to the toolbox,” the robot immediately decides to use a towel to push the screw successfully. Likewise, when tasked with “Pick up the milk carton,” it remembers to reposition the apple first before retrieving the target item. 5.3 Evaluation of Grounding VLMs through Self-Generated Memory Upon completing the task in section 5.2, the STM is autonomously transferred to the LTM for future use. Together with 96 unrelated experiences from simple tasks, we build an LTM containing 100 entries. For the baseline, we use Come Robot , which does not have access to the LTM. We first evaluate the effectiveness of the LTM by reconstructing the exact same scene with the same objects. As shown in Table 3, the robot successfully recalls the correct action from the LTM with RAG, demonstrating improved performance compared to Come Robot. We further investigate its ability to generalize. To do so, we modify the scene to create new but structurally similar scenarios, as illustrated in Figure 4. The results in Table 3 show that experience gained from one task successfully transfers to related tasks under similar conditions and significantly improves the success rate. 5.4 Ablation Study of Memory Retrieval To evaluate the effectiveness of our memory retrieval strategy, we measure the VLM’s task planning success rate (without execution) across 12 tasks using three retrieval settings, as shown in Table 4. We re-use the self-generated LTM described in section 5.3. Randomly selecting k memories (with k = 5) yields the worst performance, with a success rate of 27%. This is because the likelihood of retrieving task-relevant context is relatively low. Providing the entire LTM leads to better performance (success rate = 67%); however, unfiltered retrieval can overwhelm the model with irrelevant or distracting information, introducing unstable behavior. This aligns with prior findings that excessively long or noisy contexts can degrade model performance, as LLMs may struggle to focus on the most relevant content . In contrast, our retrieval strategy with RAG consistently improves accuracy, achieving a success rate of 89%. Most remaining failures occur when the VLM judges the 7 retrieved memory to be misaligned with the current visual scene and thus chooses to rely less on the past experience stored in LTM. The results demonstrate that incorporating image annotation consistently enhances performance. 6 Conclusion This work introduces EXPTEACH, a novel method that equips VLMs with self-generated memory to better ground them in real-world robotic systems. Empirical results show that EXPTEACH enables robots to autonomously reflect and adapt through short-term memory, leading to substantial improvements in task success rates and enabling intelligent object interactions (such as creative tool use). Additionally, extensive experimental results show that aggregating these self-generated shortterm memories grounds the VLM in its own past experience, yielding significant improvements over the state of the art in task planning when faced with new scenarios. Our work can serve as a general framework for integrating VLMs with robotic systems and is a step further towards the development of general-purpose robotic systems. 8 7 Limitations and Future Work While EXPTEACH demonstrates strong potential in grounding VLMs within robotic systems by autonomously generating memory, it still presents several limitations. First, EXPTEACH currently focuses exclusively on manipulation tasks. However, its core approach is not inherently limited to this domain, and we plan to extend it to mobile manipulation tasks in future work . Second, our current setup assumes that visual feedback alone is sufficient for understanding and decisionmaking. In practice, some real-world scenarios require feedback that cannot be captured by vision alone. Integrating additional modalities–such as tactile or auditory signals–could greatly improve the system’s capacity to interpret complex, multimodal feedback . Third, while prior work has explored aligning robotic memory with user preferences, EXPTEACH does not yet support this capability. We intend to incorporate user-aligned memory into our framework, enabling more personalized and context-aware behavior . Finally, inspired by Self-Instruct , we are also interested in enabling VLMs to autonomously propose tasks, generate instructions, and learn from the outcomes, further reducing the amount of human effort required. context: Canonical Correlation Patterns for Validating Clustering of Multivariate Time Series Isabella Degen1, Zahraa S Abdallah2, Kate Robson Brown3, and Henry W J Reeve4 1School of Computer Science, University of Bristol 2School of Engineering Mathematics and Technology, University of Bristol 3College of Engineering and Architecture, University College Dublin 4School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Nanjing July 23, 2025 ABSTRACT Clustering of multivariate time series using correlation-based methods reveals regime changes in relationships between variables across health, finance, and industrial applications. However, validating whether discovered clusters represent distinct relationships rather than arbitrary groupings remains a fundamental challenge. Existing clustering validity indices were developed for Euclidean data, and their effectiveness for correlation structures has not been systematically evaluated. Unlike Euclidean clustering, where geometric shapes provide visible discrete reference targets for objective assessment, correlation structures exist in continuous space without equivalent discrete reference patterns. We address this critical validation gap by introducing canonical correlation patterns as mathematically defined validation targets that discretise the infinite correlation space into finite, interpretable reference structures. These canonical patterns in correlation clustering serve as the equivalent of geometric shapes, enabling systematic evaluation of distance functions and validity indices for correlation-based clustering. Using synthetic datasets with perfect ground truth across controlled conditions, including distribution shifts, sparsification, and downsampling, we demonstrate that canonical patterns provide reliable validation targets, using the L1 norm as distance function for mapping and the L5 norm for calculating the silhouette width criterion and Davies-Bouldin index that show superior performance. These methods are robust to sparsification and distribution shifts, and appropriately detect correlation structure degradation under downsampling, enabling practical implementation guidelines for correlation-based clustering validation. This work establishes the methodological foundation for rigorous correlation-based clustering validation, enabling confident application in high-stakes domains while providing a template for structure-specific clustering evaluation methodologies. Keywords multivariate time series · clustering · correlation patterns · distance functions · internal validity indices · clustering validity indices · structure-based validation · clustering validation 1 Introduction Clustering is a fundamental unsupervised learning task that groups similar objects to reveal underlying structures and patterns within data . Time series clustering handles temporal data with unique characteristics such as temporal dependencies and evolving relationships and can reveal meaningful information about the behaviour of the underlying system that generated the data . Correlationbased time series clustering helps to discover relationship patterns between variables. Identifying patterns in changes in correlations has supported the discovery of new knowledge across diverse domains such as identifying market conditions in finance where asset correlation regimes change ar Xiv:2507.16497v1 [cs.LG] 22 Jul 2025 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 Figure 1: Correlation-based clustering first segments multivariate time series X when correlation regimes between variables change. Then, each segment’s (Sm) correlation matrix (Am) captures the relationships between all variate pairs (Q) during that period. Next, segments with similar correlation structures are clustered together. These clusters (Ck) are then mapped to canonical patterns (Pℓ) that serve as discrete validation targets. Finally, the canonical patterns that exist in dataset X are interpreted using domain expertise. , detecting operational states in industrial systems where changing sensor relationships indicate different system modes , or understanding gene expression in biology . The fundamental challenge in clustering is the need to be able to validate results without ground truth information. Given the many possible ways to partition a dataset, clustering validation aims to objectively distinguish meaningful patterns from arbitrary groupings . The established guiding principle is that results of higher quality have higher cohesion within clusters and better separation between clusters . When clustering Euclidean data, the quality of the result can be objectively assessed by analysing whether the clusters form visibly distinct geometrical shapes . However, correlation matrices form a continuous space that lacks such visible discrete reference targets. Consequently, when correlation matrices are grouped into clusters that are expected to represent periods of similar relationships between time series variables, there is no established systematic method to validate whether these clusters represent meaningful periods of distinct relationships or merely arbitrary collections of various correlation matrices. Figure 1 shows how a 3-variate time series dataset is segmented into subsequences when the relationships between the variates change. For each segment, the correlation matrix is calculated and then grouped into clusters of similar relationships between time series. The validation challenge is to objectively assess whether the segmentation of the time series and subsequent clustering of these segments result in optimal cohesive and well-separated clusters of different relationships. The following three gaps prevent reliable validation of correlation-based time series clustering, leading to subjective conclusions about the effectiveness of the methods and the validity of the results . First, the absence of discrete validation targets for correlation structures, analogous to geometrical shapes in the Euclidean space, prevents the formalisation of objective evaluation criteria. Second, the effectiveness of existing clustering validity indices and distance functions that assess the structural quality of clustering results without requiring ground truth has not been systematically evaluated for correlation-based clustering. Instead, these methods were developed and validated for Euclidean data . Third, impacts from real-world data complexities common in time series data, such as irregular sampling, missing data, and non-normal distributions have unknown effects on distance functions and clustering validation indices, preventing 2 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 the establishment of performance thresholds or interpretation guidelines for judging the quality of results. We solve this fundamental validation problem by introducing canonical correlation patterns as verifiable target structures. Canonical patterns discretise the infinite correlation space into mathematically defined states (strong positive, negligible, strong negative correlations between variable pairs), creating well-defined validation targets that encompass the complete correlation space in a maximally contrasted way and serve as the correlation-based clustering equivalent of geometric shapes in Euclidean clustering; see Figure 1 illustrating how the resulting clusters map to canonical patterns that serve as validation targets. Additionally, canonical patterns eliminate the need to predefine cluster numbers, as datasets naturally contain the subset of canonical patterns present in the underlying correlation dynamics, and aid in result interpretation since each canonical pattern can be assigned domain meaning by domain experts. Our work makes three key contributions: (1) formalising canonical correlation patterns as mathematical validation targets that discretise the infinite correlation space into finite, interpretable reference structures; (2) systematic empirical evaluation of the effectiveness of distance functions and validity indices for correlation matrices through controlled experiments; (3) establishing practical validation guidelines and actionable recommendations through robustness assessment across non-normal distributions, missing data, and varying completeness levels, as well as sensitivity to cluster and segment count. Together, these contributions provide the methodological foundation for rigorous correlation-based clustering validation through formalised mathematical targets, empirically validated methods, and practical implementation guidance. For scope clarification, rather than providing an exhaustive theoretical comparison of all possible distance functions, we take an empirical approach aimed at identifying reliable practical solutions that are interpretable, computationally stable, and robust to real-world data quality challenges. The methodological work described here establishes the foundations that allowed us to create the standardised algorithm evaluation protocols for correlationbased clustering using the synthetic CSTS benchmarking dataset . In CSTS, all canonical patterns are systematically represented and validated for multiple data variations, such as distribution shifts, downsampling, sparsification, and controlled degraded clustering results, providing perfect ground truth information. This allows isolating impacts of data variation on correlation patterns from limitations of clustering validation indices and enables rigorous statistical evaluation. The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on clustering applications and validation frameworks, highlighting key gaps in correlation-based clustering validation. Section 3 establishes the mathematical formulation and notation used and formalises the canonical correlation patterns as discrete clustering validation targets for the infinite correlation space. Section 4 provides the standard formulas for evaluating the discriminative power of distance functions and assessing clustering quality through external and internal validity indices. Section 5 presents our methodology, detailing how we select, evaluate, and validate distance functions for canonical pattern mapping and internal validity indices for clustering quality. Section 6 outlines the experimental setup, and Section 7 presents the results. Section 8 discusses our key findings, compares our results with previous studies, provides practical recommendations, and acknowledges the limitations of our approach while suggesting future research directions. Finally, Section 9 concludes the article. 2 Related Work Clustering is a fundamental unsupervised machine learning technique that groups similar objects to reveal the underlying structures and patterns in the data . As an established approach in data mining, clustering has become essential across numerous disciplines , applied to domains such as biology , mental health , finance  and genomics , discovering hidden structures such as patient subgroups , financial market segmentations , genomic patterns , and anomalies in control systems . The methods and challenges vary depending on the type of data that are being clustered. Time series clustering introduces unique complexities such as temporal dependencies, high dimensionality, and dynamic nature of data that are distinct from Euclidean data . These unique characteristics often require specific preprocessing and representation techniques prior to clustering, such as dimensionality reduction or feature extraction, introducing more steps that require validation . Our work focusses on correlation-based multivariate time series clustering, a feature-based approach where correlation 3 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 matrices serve as extracted features representing relationships between variates . A comprehensive review by Marti et al.  documents the methodological developments in correlation-based clustering of financial time series, mainly using network-based approaches that convert correlation matrices into distance functions for hierarchical clustering algorithms (like Minimum Spanning Trees) and their extensions (such as Planar Maximally Filtered Graphs). Other researchers take a different approach to clustering based on correlations. Chandereng and Gitter  introduced Lag Penalised Weighted Correlation (LPWC), employing a clustering similarity function (1-Pearson correlation) that groups univariate time series with similar temporal patterns even when they occur at slightly different times. Despite its utility and the prolific methods available, choosing and configuring a suitable clustering algorithm remains challenging. Many algorithms needed prior knowledge of the number of clusters and other hyperparameters that are difficult to identify and optimise, given that in real-world datasets, we apply clustering to datasets without ground truth information that would help define such parameters . Furthermore, it remains unclear which method works best for a specific dataset . Studies such as Javed et al.  and Paparrizos and Reddy  demonstrate that different datasets and problems require different clustering approaches, and Rodriguez et al.  mentions that algorithms exhibit varying sensitivities to parameter configurations. As Jaeger and Banks  notes, clustering represents an expansive domain in which practitioners must develop customised approaches for each application context. In short, the advice is "try various methods and see", which has led to the debate of whether clustering is more "art than science" . These challenges have motivated extensive research into clustering validation techniques. The field of clustering validation spans several decades. Various researchers have created different internal clustering validation indices with the goal of measuring clustering quality without using domain information such as ground truth labels that external indices make use of . Many internal clustering validity indices have been designed to assess the structural quality of clustering results and provide a measure of better within cluster cohesion and between cluster separation ; for technical background on clustering validity assessment please refer to Section 4.2. The seminal work of Milligan and Cooper  established the foundation for comparing such indices. This pioneering study introduced a seven-step process where indices that perform better are those that determine optimal cluster numbers. More recently, Vendramin et al.  and Arbelaitz et al.  extended this framework, providing detailed comparisons of the strengths and weaknesses of various internal validity indices. Vendramin et al.  validated the performance of internal validity indices beyond determining the "correct" numbers of clusters by calculating their Pearson correlations with external clustering indices. Internal indices with higher correlation with an external index were judged as superior. In a similar study, Arbelaitz et al.  evaluated internal indices using synthetic and real datasets, also stressing that grouping similar objects is more important than finding the "right" number of clusters. Both studies argue that noise might increase cluster numbers without reducing clustering quality which for them, like for many of the internal indices inventors, is related to the structure of the result. The scope of these validation studies is substantial: Vendramin et al.  evaluated 40 internal validity indices using four different hierarchical clustering algorithms, comparing the results with three external validity indices across 1080 synthetic datasets. Arbelaitz et al.  assessed 30 internal validity indices using k-means and hierarchical clustering on 720 synthetic and 20 real datasets from the UCI repository . Another study worth mentioning is Liu et al.  which followed the work of Milligan and Cooper  more closely but introduced variations in the datasets such as varying density, cluster shapes, separation, and noise. The clustering indices that are evaluated as performing best were those that achieved the optimal internal index value for the right number of clusters for the maximal number of different datasets. Significantly, all these studies concluded that no single internal validity index outperforms others across all scenarios. This finding aligns with Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem , which mathematically proves that no clustering function can simultaneously satisfy three desirable properties: scale invariance, richness, and consistency . This theoretical barrier explains why different validity indices favour different algorithms and data characteristics. In addition to using internal validity indices to evaluate structural properties, stability-based approaches assess the consistency of the results of a clustering algorithm under data perturbations . We deliberately exclude clustering stability from our validation techniques review as it primarily evaluates algorithm robustness rather than the intrinsic structural quality of the resulting clusters. 4 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 Although these comprehensive validation frameworks provide a solid foundation, they were designed using Euclidean datasets and internal validity indices have not been specifically assessed for time series clustering . In contrast to structure-based internal validation, time series clustering algorithms are typically compared by benchmarking them against classification datasets that contain ground truth information. Notable time series benchmarking studies include Javed et al. , which used a phased evaluation framework that isolated the effects of eight algorithms (including partitional, density-based, and hierarchical methods) and three distance functions (Euclidean, dynamic time warping, shapebased) on 112 datasets from the UCR archive . Their analysis found that performance variation depended more on dataset characteristics than algorithmic innovations. Similarly, the Odyssey study from Paparrizos and Reddy  analysed 80 univariate time series clustering methods across 128 datasets. Both studies used external validation indices, since the UCR datasets consist of presegmented univariate time series already assigned to classes. This validation approach, while valuable for evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of algorithms, conflates clustering and classification by assuming presegmented data with known ground truth, which introduces a critical methodological issue of classification boundaries defined by humans that do not necessarily reflect structural properties . Algorithms may perform poorly not because they fail to discover meaningful structures, but because the expected classifications might not match such structures . Additionally to evaluating clustering algorithms for their ability to discover classification labels, these benchmarking studies use real-world datasets. This is both an advantage as such data include the full complexities of time series data but they make it impossible to isolate the performance of the algorithms from the quality of the underlying structures in the data. Our work addresses the gap in correlation-based time series clustering for which distance functions and internal validity indices have not been systematically evaluated. Our perspective is that clustering is a method to find structure in data and therefore the validation techniques need to be based on the quality of the discovered structure not on domain-based labels. 3 Problem Formalisation This section establishes the mathematical formulation and notation of correlation-based clustering and formalises the canonical correlation patterns as discrete clustering validation targets for the infinite correlation space. Throughout, we shall let R denote the set of real numbers and N the set of positive integers. Given a natural number N ∈N, we let [N] := {1, . . . , N}. 3.1 Correlation-based Clustering First, we establish the notation of objects and their relations used in correlation-based clustering. Let X in RT ×V be a matrix where T ∈N is the number of observations and V ∈N is the number of variates in the time series. Given M ∈N we shall let G(M) denote the collection of segmentations into M segments. Formally, for each M ∈N the set G(M) consists of all strictly increasing sequences η = (ηm)M m=0 ∈[T]M+1 of length M +1 with η0 := 0 and ηM := T. For each m ∈[M], the values ηm−1 + 1 and ηm denote the start and end of the m-th index, respectively. We also let G := ST M=1 G(M) denote the set of all possible segmentations of a time horizon T. For each M ∈T, η ∈G(M) and m ∈[M] we let Sm ≡Sm(X, η) := X(ηm−1 + 1, . . . , ηm), (1) which takes values in R|ηm−ηm−1|×V , denote the m-th segment of X, containing sequential observations t ∈{ηm−1 + 1, . . . , ηm}. Then we shall let corr : S R∈N, R≥V RR×V →RV ×V denote the Spearman rank correlation  mapping from R × V matrices ˜X to the corresponding V × V correlation matrix A. The tied values are assigned average ranks, and the Spearman correlation is calculated using the standard tie-corrected formula. For our application of corr, we define the correlation coefficient aij := 0 for the cases of Sm when exactly one of the variates i or j is constant, and aij := 1 when both are constant. The image of corr is contained within the subspace AV ⊆RV ×V consisting of symmetric positive semi-definite matrices with unit diagonal and elements aij ∈[−1, 1] for i, j ∈V and i ̸= j. Note that AV forms a Q-dimensional subspace where Q := V (V −1)/2 is the number of unique pairs of 5 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 variates. As such, we sometimes represent elements of AV by vectors in RQ, where the correlation coefficients aij are ordered lexicographically a U := [a12, a13, ..., a(V −1)V ]. For each segment Sm where m ∈[M], we write Am ≡Am(X, η) := corr(Sm), (2) for its correlation matrix. Next, we write K(M, K) for the set of all clusterings Φ := (ϕ1, . . . , ϕK) which are sequences of K disjoint non-empty subsets of [M] whose union is S Φ = ϕ1 ∪. . . ∪ϕK = [M]. Additionally, we let SC(M, K) denote the set of all segmented clusterings which are tuples of the form π := (η, Φ), (3) where η ∈G(M) and Φ ∈K(M, K) is a clustering of these segments. Furthermore, given π ∈SC(M, K) and m ∈[M] and k ∈[K] we let Ck(π) := {Am : m ∈ϕk}, (4) denote a cluster where ϕk ∈Φ. Finally, to compare how similar two matrices are, we shall leverage a non-negative function d : AV × AV →R≥0 on the space AV as distance function. Given correlation matrices Ax, Ay ∈AV we view d(Ax, Ay) as quantifying the degree of dissimilarity between Ax and Ay. In practice many examples of d will be metrics, yet we require no further properties beyond non-negativity. We provide the definitions for the various distance functions employed in Appendix B. 3.2 Canonical Patterns Next, we formalise the canonical correlation patterns as discrete mathematical validation targets for correlation matrices that underpin our method for correlation-based clustering validation. Let P ∈AV denote a canonical pattern with elements pij ∈{−1, 0, 1} for i, j ∈[V ] and i ̸= j. Each canonical pattern Pℓwith ℓ∈[L] represents a unique idealised correlation structure capturing strong positive correlation, no correlation, or strong negative correlation between the Q unique variate pairs. The total number of different canonical patterns is L := 3Q. A canonical pattern Pℓmust be positive semi-definite to be a valid correlation matrix. To fulfil this requirement, we define a relaxed discretisation criterion where P′ ℓis considered equivalent to its canonical form Pℓ, if P′ ℓis positive semi-definite after adjusting its correlation coefficients within tolerance bands B := {[−1, −0.7], [−0.2, 0.2], [0.7, 1]}. Canonical patterns Pℓthat cannot be made positive semi-definite after this relaxation within B are invalid. The tolerance bands B represent practical thresholds that continue to clearly distinguish between strong negative, negligible, and strong positive correlation coefficients, while respecting the geometry of the correlation space AV . This relaxation process determines which of the L theoretical patterns yield valid correlation matrices, resulting in L′ < L relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓwhere ℓ∈[L′]. To facilitate human interpretation, we use the idealised Pℓto represent a pattern. For calculations, we use the corresponding relaxed form P′ ℓ, see Appendix A for a list of the 23 valid canonical patterns out of the 27 possible and their relaxed form for three time series variates. Let ψ : AV 7→{P′ ℓ: ℓ∈[L′]} denote the canonical pattern mapping ψ(Am) := min argmin ℓ∈[L′] {d(Am, P′ ℓ)} (5) that associates a correlation matrix Am with its closest relaxed canonical pattern. Here, ‘min’ ensures that the ties are broken by selecting the smallest index ℓ. The canonical pattern mapping ψ provides a natural basis for constructing a clustering Φ. A possible clustering strategy is to group correlation matrices in such a way that for k ∈[K] we have ϕk := {m ∈[M] : ψ(Am) = P′ ℓ} , (6) where ℓ∈[L′]. Under such an approach, canonical patterns P′ ℓserve as discrete, idealised, interpretable target clusters of the clustering Φ. Each cluster ϕk then consists of all segment indices m whose correlation matrices map to the same relaxed canonical pattern P′ ℓ. Note that K ≤L′ as not all ℓ∈[L′] need to be present in a given time series X. 6 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 3.3 Level Sets for Canonical Patterns Finally, we introduce level sets that enable a systematic evaluation of distance functions by grouping canonical patterns according to their theoretical similarity. Let d L1 : AV × AV →R≥0 denote the L1 distance between canonical patterns so that d L1(Px, Py) := V X i=1 V X j>i |pxij −pyij|, (7) for pattern indices x, y ∈[L′]. Let DL1 := {δ ∈R : ∃x, y ∈[L′], d L1(Px, Py) = δ} denote the ordered sequence of achievable L1 distances between valid canonical patterns. The theoretical maximum δmax is bounded by V (V −1), although this δmax may not be achievable due to the constraints on valid correlation matrices. To give an example, with three time series variates (V = 3) the sequence becomes DL1 = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, where a distance of 1 represents one coefficient changing by ±1, a distance of 2 represents either two coefficients changing by ±1 or one coefficient flipping sign, and so forth. The theoretical maximum distance of 6 for V = 3 cannot be achieved while only retaining the canonical patterns Pℓthat can satisfy the tolerance bands B and be a valid correlation matrix Am. For each potential distance value δ ∈DL1, we define the level set Lδ as Lδ := {(x, y) : x, y ∈[L′], d L1(Px, Py) = δ}. (8) The collection {Lδ}δ∈DL1 groups pattern index pairs (x, y) by their L1 distance, with L0 containing indices of identical patterns, L1 containing indices of patterns where one correlation coefficient differs by ±1, and so forth. This creates a natural ordering between the level sets, while all the pattern pairs within each Lδ are theoretically equivalent. 4 Evaluation Reference Formulas This section provides established formulas for evaluating the performance of distance functions and assessing clustering quality, providing the mathematical foundation for our methodology. 4.1 Discriminative Power The effectiveness of a distance function d to map empirical correlation matrices Am to their closest canonical patterns P′ ℓ(see Section 3.2) can be evaluated using multiple complementary approaches. We investigate how well a distance function distinguishes across all the canonical patterns, how consistent distances are within a level set Lδ (see Section 3.3) and how well a distance function performs this mapping in the basic 1NN classifier where all the neighbours have been hardcoded to be the canonical patterns. In this section, we provide the established formulas used for these evaluations. 4.1.1 Overall Discriminative Power We use Shannon’s entropy  to evaluate the overall variability of distances. Given a finite number of distances γ ∈D, where D is a multi set, Shannon’s entropy is defined as HD := k X i=1 p(γi) log2(1/p(γi)), (9) where k is the number of bins, γi are the distances falling into bin i, and p(γi) is the relative frequency of the distances in bin i (empirical estimate of the probability mass function for the distances γ ∈D). For the overall discriminative power of a distance function d, we consider all distances. Therefore, D := {γ ∈R≥0 : γ = d(Ax, P′ y)}, where x ∈[M], y ∈[L′], and then |D| = M × L′. The larger HD, the more uncertain and random the observed distances are, which is desirable. 7 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 4.1.2 Level Set Discriminative Power Level sets Lδ (see Section 3.3) lend interpretable properties to evaluate the suitability of a distance function d to map correlation matrices to canonical patterns (see Eq. 5). We expect the distance d between an empirical correlation matrix Am and a canonical pattern P′ ℓto be smaller, the closer the canonical pattern is to the pattern used to create the empirical correlation matrix. We also use Shannon’s entropy to evaluate the similarity of distances within the level sets. For the analysis of the level sets of a distance function d, we consider the subset of distances γ ∈Dδ where Dδ ⊂D for the respective level set Lδ defined as Dδ := {γ ∈R≥0 : γ = d(Ax, P′ y)}, where x ∈[M] and y ∈[L′] such that d L1(Px, Py) = δ, where Px was the canonical pattern used to generate the segment from which the empirical correlation matrix Ax was calculated and Py is the relaxed canonical pattern P′ y we calculate the distance for. The closer to zero HDδ is, the more uniform the observed distances within the level set, which is desirable. The average entropy for all level sets is defined as HL := 1 |DL1| X δ∈DL1 HDδ. (10) Furthermore, the average rate of increase in distances from level set to level set is defined as RL := 1 |DL1| X δ∈DL1 |µLδ −µLδ+1|, (11) where µLδ is the mean distance for the level set Lδ for a distance function. The average rate measures the mean absolute difference in distances between consecutive level sets. 4.1.3 Canonical Pattern Classification Power The ability of a distance function to best map correlation matrices to their matching canonical pattern can be seen as a classification problem. For this we "train" 1NN, the most basic classifier , on the canonical patterns. In this scenario, the neighbours are hardcoded to the canonical patterns. We use this 1NN classifier to assign each empirical correlation matrix to its closest relaxed canonical pattern using a distance function d. Our aim is to identify both distance functions that can discriminate between the different canonical correlation patterns and map empirical correlation matrices to their canonical patterns, as well as internal validity indices that quantify the quality of a particular segmented clustering. The distance functions and internal indices selected must provide good interpretability, computational stability, and robustness to common variations in the quality of real-life data. For both evaluations, we follow a systematic three-stage methodology in which we first select candidates; second empirically evaluate their performance; and third, statistically validate whether there are superior options. We recognise that statistically significant differences may not always translate to meaningful practical improvements and therefore evaluate both practical and statistical differences between candidates. Importantly, we assess distance function performance in two distinct contexts. First, we evaluate their ability to directly discriminate between canonical correlation patterns. Second, we evaluate how these same distance functions perform when embedded within internal validity indices for clustering quality assessment. As we demonstrate, optimal distance functions may differ between these contexts. For statistical testing, we employ a two-phase approach (exploratory and confirmatory) to reduce false discoveries, organising the tests into six families to control Type I error rates . We conduct the experiments using the CSTS benchmark datasets , which provides validated ground truth clusterings for all canonical patterns under normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified data conditions. CSTS further provides controlled degraded quality clustering as well as reduced cluster and segment count versions to enable a thorough investigation of the effectiveness and potential biases of the validation methods. 5.1 Canonical Pattern Mapping Assessment Our aim in this section is to identify which distance functions best map empirical correlation matrices to their underlying canonical patterns. We describe how we select candidate distance functions and then evaluate their ability to distinguish between different canonical correlation patterns, as well as validate whether there is a superior distance function. 5.1.1 Distance Function Selection We select distance functions using the following four key principles: 1. Interpretability: The distance function must follow human intuition about similarity and differences between correlation matrices Am and canonical patterns Pℓ. The distance function should allow meaningful interpretations of which cluster Ck(π) best fits each observed correlation matrix Am and which cluster best fits a canonical pattern Pℓ. 2. Discriminative Power: The distance function must be able to effectively and reliably distinguish between the different canonical patterns Pℓand assign correlation matrices Am to their closest canonical pattern Pℓ, see the canonical pattern mapping equation 5. Each canonical pattern should be equally distinguishable. 3. Computational Stability: The distance function must be numerically stable. This includes dealing with very small eigenvalues λi and singular correlation matrices, which are both common in the relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓ. The computation time needs to be feasible on standard hardware, prioritising result quality over processing speed. 4. Robustness: The distance function needs to be able to handle real-world challenges such as varying segment lengths, irregular sampling, and non-normal distributions of the time series variates without the need for manual parameter tuning, which is not possible without knowing the ground truth. Following these four principles, we select the vector-based distance functions Lp norm, Lp norm with reference vector, dot transformed Lp norm, and the matrix-based distance functions Log Frobenius norm and Förstner metric (all defined in Appendix B). We focus on vector-based distance functions 11 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 because of their direct quantification of the differences in correlation coefficients and easy geometrical interpretation. We include matrix-based distance functions because they, to varying degrees, capture the geometry of correlation matrices, which could be advantageous. Our selection includes distance functions that are directly applicable to correlation matrices without requiring parameter tuning. This excludes time series specific distance function like Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), which requires parameter tuning and measures distance between time series observations rather than correlations. We also focus on distance functions with direct geometric interpretation for correlation matrices, excluding probabilistic and graph-based approaches. 5.1.2 Distance Function Evaluation We systematically evaluate the performance of the selected distance functions to identify which dissimilarity function best satisfies our four key principles to map empirical correlation matrices to canonical patterns. Each distance function is assessed against criteria derived from the principles of interpretability and discriminative power, with robustness and computational stability serving as a prerequisite for inclusion; see details in Section 6.2. For interpretability, we evaluate whether distance functions produce intuitive mappings between empirical correlation matrices and canonical patterns. This includes evaluating distance consistency within level sets (see Eq. 8) and meaningful separation between level sets. For discriminative power, we assess each distance function’s ability to reliably distinguish between canonical patterns and correctly assign empirical correlation matrices to their closest canonical pattern. This evaluation focusses on the distance function’s capacity to maintain clear boundaries between different canonical patterns and accurately assign empirical correlation matrices. We rank distance functions based on their performance for each of these criteria, providing both relative comparisons between distance functions and overall performance evaluation to ensure that high-ranking distance functions demonstrate genuine effectiveness rather than merely superior relative performance. The evaluation is carried out separately for normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified data conditions to assess robustness and identify distance functions that maintain consistent performance under real-world challenges. 5.1.3 Statistical Validation To statistically validate whether the distance function ranked highest is superior, we use Wilcoxon signed rank tests  to compare the distance function ranks for each subject. These tests constitute Family 1 of our six-family statistical testing framework, specifically designed to control Type I error rates when determining which distance functions best map correlation matrices to canonical patterns. In the exploratory phase, we employ a step-down procedure starting with the two best-ranked distance functions and expanding comparisons until significant differences are found. We allow for different distance functions to achieve significantly lower ranks for different data variants. Based on exploratory findings, we preregister the directional hypotheses for confirmatory tests , see Table 1. 5.2 Internal Validity Index Assessment Having established optimal distance functions for canonical pattern discrimination, we now aim to identify which distance functions optimise the performance of the internal validity index and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable quantification of clustering quality with minimal bias. We first describe how we select candidate internal clustering validity indices and then evaluate using different distance functions their ability to reliably quantify the quality of a segmented clustering (see Equation 3), as well as validate whether there is a superior distance function and internal index combination. 5.2.1 Index Selection We select the internal validity indices to evaluate based on their performance in previous comprehensive evaluation studies by Vendramin et al.  and Arbelaitz et al.  as well as based on their popularity in clustering. Due to our canonical pattern approach of defining an upper bound for the possible number of patterns in a dataset, it is important that the number of clusters K and the number 12 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 of segments M do not affect the performance of the internal validity index, as not every canonical pattern will be present in every dataset despite the clustering being of equal high quality. 5.2.2 Index Evaluation We evaluate the selected internal indices to determine which distance functions optimise internal validity index performance and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable clustering quality assessment with minimal bias. We systematically evaluate both objectives for each data variant to understand how the choice of distance function affects index performance and how different indices behave under varying conditions. We evaluate how different distance functions affect internal validity index performance from two complementary perspectives. First, we assess each distance function’s ability to produce optimal raw index values for the highest-quality segmented clustering (ground-truth perfect clustering). Second, we evaluate how well each distance function enables indices to correlate with the Jaccard index, measuring the index’s ability to distinguish between different clustering quality levels. The latter perspective shows how validation without labels (internal clustering validation) matches validation using ground truth label information (external clustering validation, not available in real-world settings). We independently assess these two perspectives for each data variant and internal validity index, then synthesise the results to identify optimal distance functions. When optimal distance functions differ between raw performance and correlation performance, we examine the implications of this divergence from a practical viewpoint. Using the optimal distance functions identified above, we assess the reliability and bias of the internal validity indices. We evaluate the sensitivity of the index to varying numbers of clusters and segments by working with reduced versions of our data variants. Additionally, we synthesise results across all data variants (normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified) to assess the robustness of each index to different data characteristics and pattern degradation conditions. 5.2.3 Statistical Validation To statistically validate whether there is a superior distance function for the validity indices and an overall superior validity index, we use Wilcoxon signed rank tests to compare the evaluation results for each subject . These tests constitute Families 2-6 of our six-family statistical testing framework. We first establish which distance function and internal index combinations achieve sufficient correlation strength to warrant detailed comparative analysis. We apply a viability threshold that requires Pearson’s mean correlation |r| > 0.5 between the internal indices and the Jaccard index for each subject within each data variant, based on sample size calculations to ensure adequate statistical power. Based on viable combinations from this filtering, we define the five families (2-6) comparing the internal indices SWC and DBI, which pass this correlation viability threshold. Family 2 evaluates which distance function achieves significantly better ground truth values for SWC and DBI, while Family 3 evaluates which distance function achieves significantly stronger correlation between SWC/DBI and the Jaccard index. Family 4 examines whether SWC or DBI correlates more strongly with the Jaccard index, Family 5 examines the impacts of cluster count reduction, and Family 6 evaluates the effects of segment count reduction. In the exploratory phase, we employ a step-down procedure starting with the two best performing distance functions and internal indices, respectively, expanding comparisons until significant differences are found. We allow for different distance functions and internal indices to achieve significantly lower ranks for different data variants. Based on these exploratory findings, we preregister the directional hypotheses for confirmatory tests using hierarchical testing procedures , see Tables 2 to 6. 6 Experimental Setup We describe the experimental setup in four parts. First, we describe the CSTS benchmark dataset used for all experiments.
