A 110, 022606 . 17 Appendix A: Variational Quantum Imaginary Time Evolution (Var QITE) In this method, the approximate Gibbs state is evaluated using PQCs that implements variational quantum imaginary time evolution based on Mc Lachlan’s variational principle . A brief explanation of how Var QITE is used to approximate the Gibbs state of the Hamiltonian is presented below. For an initial state, |ψ0⟩, the imaginary time (τ = it) evolution (ITE) with respect to the Hamiltonian, H(⃗h), non-unitarily maps the state to, |ψτ⟩= e−H(⃗h)τ |ψ0⟩ q ⟨ψ0| e−2H(⃗h)τ |ψ0⟩ , (A1) and follows Wick-rotated Schrodinger’s equation, d |ψτ⟩ dτ = −(H(⃗h) −Eτ) |ψτ⟩, where Eτ = ⟨ψτ| H(⃗h) |ψτ⟩is the system’s energy. If the initial state |ψ0⟩is taken to be a purification of the maximally mixed state, ρ = Tr A |ψ0⟩⟨ψ0| = I/d, where A represents the ancilla subsystem, and the imaginary time evolution is kept as τ →1/2T = β/2 for the system, then Eq. (A1) yields a purification of the Gibbs state defined in Eq. (1). The ITE state cannot be directly implemented on a quantum circuit because of the non-unitary nature of evolution. However, Mc Ardle et al. showed that the ITE can be implemented on a hybrid gate-based quantum computer using Mc Lachlan’s variational principle. The main idea here is as follows. First, the state |ψτ⟩is approximated by defining a parametrized trial state : |ϕ(⃗ω(τ))⟩= U(⃗ω(τ)) |0⟩, where U(⃗ω(τ)) = UN(ωn)UN−1(ωN−1).....Uk(ωk)....U1(ω1) are the set of parametrized single or two-qubit gates with parameters ⃗ω(τ). Since the goal is the preparation of Gibbs state and this requires purification of maximally mixed states as the initial boundary condition, the state |ϕ(⃗ω(τ))⟩is defined over a PQC with a total of n + nancilla qubits. The initial value of parameters of the unitaries are chosen such that, |ϕ(⃗ω(τ = 0))⟩= U(⃗ω(τ = 0)) |0⟩⊗2n = ϕ+ ⊗n , where |ϕ+⟩⊗n = 1 √ 2(|00⟩+ |11⟩) is the Bell state. Here, in each Bell state |ϕ+⟩, the first qubit belongs to the system, while the second qubit serves as an ancilla. Tracing out the ancillas from |ϕ(ω(0))⟩results in the maximally mixed state; I 2n . Further, the ITE of |ϕ(⃗ω(τ))⟩is done by implementing Mc Lachlan variational principle, δ||( ∂ ∂τ + H(⃗h) −Eτ) |ϕ(⃗ω(τ))⟩|| = 0, using quantum circuits for τ = β/2. The state, Trb[|ϕ(⃗ω(τ = β/2))⟩] at the end of τ = β/2 evolution gives the approximation to the Gibbs state of our system Hamiltonian, H(⃗h). For more detailed calculations, please refer to Zoufal et al.  and Mc Ardle et al. . In this work, the technique has been adapted solely for comparative study using specific examples, with the variational quantum imaginary time evolution simulated using the built-in library available in Qiskit. Appendix B: Overview of Classical and Quantum Boltzmann Machines This section provides brief overview of classical and quantum Boltzmann machines, both of which fundamentally rely on the system’s Gibbs state. 1. Classical Boltzmann Machine Classical Boltzmann Machines are a type of energybased stochastic neural network inspired by statistical mechanics. They learn complex probability distributions over input data. The network consists of interconnected nodes of visible and hidden neurons, that commonly represent binary states. The input data is represented using the visible neurons while the latent features in the input data is learned by the hidden neurons. Figure 14, shows a type of Boltzmann machine known as Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) where connections exist between visible and hidden neurons but not among neurons within the same layer. The entire network is described by an energy function, E(v, h) = −PNv i=1 aivi −PNh i=1 bihi −P i,j wi,jvihj, where v is the visible unit, h is the hidden unit, Nv represents the number of visible units, Nh represents the number of hidden units, ai and bi are the visible and hidden unit biases, and wi,j is the connection weight between visible and hidden neurons. The probability distribution over possible unit configurations is represented by the Boltzmann distribution, P(v, h) = e−βE(v,h)/ P v,h e−βE(v,h), which characterizes the state of the system at finite temperature, T. During training, the temperature controls the level of stochasticity in the model, with higher temperatures leading to more uniform sampling across configurations, while lower temperatures bias the system toward lower energy (more probable) states. The weights connecting the visible and hidden neurons and the biases are trained so that the probability distribution of the target input data is accurately represented by P(v) = P h e−βE(v,h)/ P v,h e−βE(v,h). Boltzmann machines are used in various applications, including dimensionality reduction , feature learning , collaborative filtering , and pretraining of deep learning networks . 18 Visible Units Hidden units Input data Output data FIG. 14. Restricted Boltzmann Machine : The figure illustrates the architecture of a classical restricted Boltzmann machine, where connections exist between visible and hidden neurons but not among neurons within the same layer. ai and bi are the biases of visible and hidden neurons, and wi,j are the connection weights between hidden and visible neurons. The input data is mapped to the visible neurons. The hidden neurons learn the latent features in the input data by adjusting the connection weights and biases. The output is then obtained by sampling the visible layer after a round-trip of Gibbs sampling, where information is propagated from the visible to hidden layer and then back to the visible layer. This reconstructed visible state serves as the model’s output, enabling it to generate samples, reconstruct inputs, or estimate probability distributions over input data. 2. Quantum Boltzmann Machine (QBM) The quantum version of this classical architecture is known as the Quantum Boltzmann Machine. The energy function representing the network structure of classical BM shown in Fig. 14, is replaced by the parametrized Hamiltonian, H(⃗h) = p−1 X i=0 hiσi, (B1) where visible and hidden units are now qubits defined by the Pauli matrices σx, σy and σz , ⃗h = (h1, h2, ...hp) ϵ Rp are the trainable coefficients of the Hamiltonian and σi = ⊗n−1 j=0 σj i with σ’s as the Pauli matrices and σj i ϵ I, X, Y, Z. The visible qubits are those that are used to model the input data and measure the model output, while the hidden qubits are those that represent the latent features. In analogy with classical BM, the aim of QBM is to learn the parameters, ⃗h, such that the probability distribution of the Gibbs state of the Hamiltonian H(⃗h), approximates the target distributions. With the inclusion of non-commuting terms in the Hamiltonian which are absent in classical Boltzmann machines, QBMs have the potential for greater expressive power, enabling them to model a broader class of complex data distributions. For a configuration |v⟩of the visible qubits, a projective measurement on this visible state is represented as ˆΠv = |v⟩⟨v|v⊗Ih, where v and h indicate the visible and hidden subsystems, respectively. The marginal probability of observing the visible configuration v is then given by, pv(⃗h) = Tr[ˆΠvρ(⃗h)], where ρ(⃗h) = e−β ˆ H(⃗h)/Tr[e−β ˆ H(⃗h)] is the Gibbs state of the full Hamiltonian which includes both the visible and hidden qubits. If pdata is the probability distribution that represents the input data, then the training of QBM involves minimizing the distance between pdata and pv(⃗h). The distance between two probability distributions is typically quantified by the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, L(⃗h) = X v pdata log pdata pv(⃗h) . The KL divergence always takes a nonnegative value, L(⃗h) ≥0, with L(⃗h) = 0 when pdata = pv(⃗h). When the input data is provided as an encoded quantum state ρdata, the relative quantum entropy S(ρdata||ρ(⃗h)) = Tr[ρdata log ρdata −ρdata log ρ(⃗h)], is used to quantify the difference between the QBM-modeled data and the input target data . Minimization of the KL divergence or relative entropy is done on a classical  or quantum hardware  by evaluating their respective first-order derivatives with respect to coefficient ⃗h of the Hamiltonian . Furthermore, the optimization is carried out by updating the Hamiltonian parameters based on these gradients as follows, ⃗h′ = ⃗h + η∂⃗h L(⃗h), where η is the learning rate. In this paper, we consider training the QBM with only visible units using our proposed meta-algorithms for Gibbs state preparation. The computation of the gradients of the loss function is done using numerical differentiation. context: Canonical Correlation Patterns for Validating Clustering of Multivariate Time Series Isabella Degen1, Zahraa S Abdallah2, Kate Robson Brown3, and Henry W J Reeve4 1School of Computer Science, University of Bristol 2School of Engineering Mathematics and Technology, University of Bristol 3College of Engineering and Architecture, University College Dublin 4School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Nanjing July 23, 2025 ABSTRACT Clustering of multivariate time series using correlation-based methods reveals regime changes in relationships between variables across health, finance, and industrial applications. However, validating whether discovered clusters represent distinct relationships rather than arbitrary groupings remains a fundamental challenge. Existing clustering validity indices were developed for Euclidean data, and their effectiveness for correlation structures has not been systematically evaluated. Unlike Euclidean clustering, where geometric shapes provide visible discrete reference targets for objective assessment, correlation structures exist in continuous space without equivalent discrete reference patterns. We address this critical validation gap by introducing canonical correlation patterns as mathematically defined validation targets that discretise the infinite correlation space into finite, interpretable reference structures. These canonical patterns in correlation clustering serve as the equivalent of geometric shapes, enabling systematic evaluation of distance functions and validity indices for correlation-based clustering. Using synthetic datasets with perfect ground truth across controlled conditions, including distribution shifts, sparsification, and downsampling, we demonstrate that canonical patterns provide reliable validation targets, using the L1 norm as distance function for mapping and the L5 norm for calculating the silhouette width criterion and Davies-Bouldin index that show superior performance. These methods are robust to sparsification and distribution shifts, and appropriately detect correlation structure degradation under downsampling, enabling practical implementation guidelines for correlation-based clustering validation. This work establishes the methodological foundation for rigorous correlation-based clustering validation, enabling confident application in high-stakes domains while providing a template for structure-specific clustering evaluation methodologies. Keywords multivariate time series · clustering · correlation patterns · distance functions · internal validity indices · clustering validity indices · structure-based validation · clustering validation 1 Introduction Clustering is a fundamental unsupervised learning task that groups similar objects to reveal underlying structures and patterns within data . Time series clustering handles temporal data with unique characteristics such as temporal dependencies and evolving relationships and can reveal meaningful information about the behaviour of the underlying system that generated the data . Correlationbased time series clustering helps to discover relationship patterns between variables. Identifying patterns in changes in correlations has supported the discovery of new knowledge across diverse domains such as identifying market conditions in finance where asset correlation regimes change ar Xiv:2507.16497v1 [cs.LG] 22 Jul 2025 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 Figure 1: Correlation-based clustering first segments multivariate time series X when correlation regimes between variables change. Then, each segment’s (Sm) correlation matrix (Am) captures the relationships between all variate pairs (Q) during that period. Next, segments with similar correlation structures are clustered together. These clusters (Ck) are then mapped to canonical patterns (Pℓ) that serve as discrete validation targets. Finally, the canonical patterns that exist in dataset X are interpreted using domain expertise. , detecting operational states in industrial systems where changing sensor relationships indicate different system modes , or understanding gene expression in biology . The fundamental challenge in clustering is the need to be able to validate results without ground truth information. Given the many possible ways to partition a dataset, clustering validation aims to objectively distinguish meaningful patterns from arbitrary groupings . The established guiding principle is that results of higher quality have higher cohesion within clusters and better separation between clusters . When clustering Euclidean data, the quality of the result can be objectively assessed by analysing whether the clusters form visibly distinct geometrical shapes . However, correlation matrices form a continuous space that lacks such visible discrete reference targets. Consequently, when correlation matrices are grouped into clusters that are expected to represent periods of similar relationships between time series variables, there is no established systematic method to validate whether these clusters represent meaningful periods of distinct relationships or merely arbitrary collections of various correlation matrices. Figure 1 shows how a 3-variate time series dataset is segmented into subsequences when the relationships between the variates change. For each segment, the correlation matrix is calculated and then grouped into clusters of similar relationships between time series. The validation challenge is to objectively assess whether the segmentation of the time series and subsequent clustering of these segments result in optimal cohesive and well-separated clusters of different relationships. The following three gaps prevent reliable validation of correlation-based time series clustering, leading to subjective conclusions about the effectiveness of the methods and the validity of the results . First, the absence of discrete validation targets for correlation structures, analogous to geometrical shapes in the Euclidean space, prevents the formalisation of objective evaluation criteria. Second, the effectiveness of existing clustering validity indices and distance functions that assess the structural quality of clustering results without requiring ground truth has not been systematically evaluated for correlation-based clustering. Instead, these methods were developed and validated for Euclidean data . Third, impacts from real-world data complexities common in time series data, such as irregular sampling, missing data, and non-normal distributions have unknown effects on distance functions and clustering validation indices, preventing 2 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 the establishment of performance thresholds or interpretation guidelines for judging the quality of results. We solve this fundamental validation problem by introducing canonical correlation patterns as verifiable target structures. Canonical patterns discretise the infinite correlation space into mathematically defined states (strong positive, negligible, strong negative correlations between variable pairs), creating well-defined validation targets that encompass the complete correlation space in a maximally contrasted way and serve as the correlation-based clustering equivalent of geometric shapes in Euclidean clustering; see Figure 1 illustrating how the resulting clusters map to canonical patterns that serve as validation targets. Additionally, canonical patterns eliminate the need to predefine cluster numbers, as datasets naturally contain the subset of canonical patterns present in the underlying correlation dynamics, and aid in result interpretation since each canonical pattern can be assigned domain meaning by domain experts. Our work makes three key contributions: (1) formalising canonical correlation patterns as mathematical validation targets that discretise the infinite correlation space into finite, interpretable reference structures; (2) systematic empirical evaluation of the effectiveness of distance functions and validity indices for correlation matrices through controlled experiments; (3) establishing practical validation guidelines and actionable recommendations through robustness assessment across non-normal distributions, missing data, and varying completeness levels, as well as sensitivity to cluster and segment count. Together, these contributions provide the methodological foundation for rigorous correlation-based clustering validation through formalised mathematical targets, empirically validated methods, and practical implementation guidance. For scope clarification, rather than providing an exhaustive theoretical comparison of all possible distance functions, we take an empirical approach aimed at identifying reliable practical solutions that are interpretable, computationally stable, and robust to real-world data quality challenges. The methodological work described here establishes the foundations that allowed us to create the standardised algorithm evaluation protocols for correlationbased clustering using the synthetic CSTS benchmarking dataset . In CSTS, all canonical patterns are systematically represented and validated for multiple data variations, such as distribution shifts, downsampling, sparsification, and controlled degraded clustering results, providing perfect ground truth information. This allows isolating impacts of data variation on correlation patterns from limitations of clustering validation indices and enables rigorous statistical evaluation. The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on clustering applications and validation frameworks, highlighting key gaps in correlation-based clustering validation. Section 3 establishes the mathematical formulation and notation used and formalises the canonical correlation patterns as discrete clustering validation targets for the infinite correlation space. Section 4 provides the standard formulas for evaluating the discriminative power of distance functions and assessing clustering quality through external and internal validity indices. Section 5 presents our methodology, detailing how we select, evaluate, and validate distance functions for canonical pattern mapping and internal validity indices for clustering quality. Section 6 outlines the experimental setup, and Section 7 presents the results. Section 8 discusses our key findings, compares our results with previous studies, provides practical recommendations, and acknowledges the limitations of our approach while suggesting future research directions. Finally, Section 9 concludes the article. 2 Related Work Clustering is a fundamental unsupervised machine learning technique that groups similar objects to reveal the underlying structures and patterns in the data . As an established approach in data mining, clustering has become essential across numerous disciplines , applied to domains such as biology , mental health , finance  and genomics , discovering hidden structures such as patient subgroups , financial market segmentations , genomic patterns , and anomalies in control systems . The methods and challenges vary depending on the type of data that are being clustered. Time series clustering introduces unique complexities such as temporal dependencies, high dimensionality, and dynamic nature of data that are distinct from Euclidean data . These unique characteristics often require specific preprocessing and representation techniques prior to clustering, such as dimensionality reduction or feature extraction, introducing more steps that require validation . Our work focusses on correlation-based multivariate time series clustering, a feature-based approach where correlation 3 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 matrices serve as extracted features representing relationships between variates . A comprehensive review by Marti et al.  documents the methodological developments in correlation-based clustering of financial time series, mainly using network-based approaches that convert correlation matrices into distance functions for hierarchical clustering algorithms (like Minimum Spanning Trees) and their extensions (such as Planar Maximally Filtered Graphs). Other researchers take a different approach to clustering based on correlations. Chandereng and Gitter  introduced Lag Penalised Weighted Correlation (LPWC), employing a clustering similarity function (1-Pearson correlation) that groups univariate time series with similar temporal patterns even when they occur at slightly different times. Despite its utility and the prolific methods available, choosing and configuring a suitable clustering algorithm remains challenging. Many algorithms needed prior knowledge of the number of clusters and other hyperparameters that are difficult to identify and optimise, given that in real-world datasets, we apply clustering to datasets without ground truth information that would help define such parameters . Furthermore, it remains unclear which method works best for a specific dataset . Studies such as Javed et al.  and Paparrizos and Reddy  demonstrate that different datasets and problems require different clustering approaches, and Rodriguez et al.  mentions that algorithms exhibit varying sensitivities to parameter configurations. As Jaeger and Banks  notes, clustering represents an expansive domain in which practitioners must develop customised approaches for each application context. In short, the advice is "try various methods and see", which has led to the debate of whether clustering is more "art than science" . These challenges have motivated extensive research into clustering validation techniques. The field of clustering validation spans several decades. Various researchers have created different internal clustering validation indices with the goal of measuring clustering quality without using domain information such as ground truth labels that external indices make use of . Many internal clustering validity indices have been designed to assess the structural quality of clustering results and provide a measure of better within cluster cohesion and between cluster separation ; for technical background on clustering validity assessment please refer to Section 4.2. The seminal work of Milligan and Cooper  established the foundation for comparing such indices. This pioneering study introduced a seven-step process where indices that perform better are those that determine optimal cluster numbers. More recently, Vendramin et al.  and Arbelaitz et al.  extended this framework, providing detailed comparisons of the strengths and weaknesses of various internal validity indices. Vendramin et al.  validated the performance of internal validity indices beyond determining the "correct" numbers of clusters by calculating their Pearson correlations with external clustering indices. Internal indices with higher correlation with an external index were judged as superior. In a similar study, Arbelaitz et al.  evaluated internal indices using synthetic and real datasets, also stressing that grouping similar objects is more important than finding the "right" number of clusters. Both studies argue that noise might increase cluster numbers without reducing clustering quality which for them, like for many of the internal indices inventors, is related to the structure of the result. The scope of these validation studies is substantial: Vendramin et al.  evaluated 40 internal validity indices using four different hierarchical clustering algorithms, comparing the results with three external validity indices across 1080 synthetic datasets. Arbelaitz et al.  assessed 30 internal validity indices using k-means and hierarchical clustering on 720 synthetic and 20 real datasets from the UCI repository . Another study worth mentioning is Liu et al.  which followed the work of Milligan and Cooper  more closely but introduced variations in the datasets such as varying density, cluster shapes, separation, and noise. The clustering indices that are evaluated as performing best were those that achieved the optimal internal index value for the right number of clusters for the maximal number of different datasets. Significantly, all these studies concluded that no single internal validity index outperforms others across all scenarios. This finding aligns with Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem , which mathematically proves that no clustering function can simultaneously satisfy three desirable properties: scale invariance, richness, and consistency . This theoretical barrier explains why different validity indices favour different algorithms and data characteristics. In addition to using internal validity indices to evaluate structural properties, stability-based approaches assess the consistency of the results of a clustering algorithm under data perturbations . We deliberately exclude clustering stability from our validation techniques review as it primarily evaluates algorithm robustness rather than the intrinsic structural quality of the resulting clusters. 4 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 Although these comprehensive validation frameworks provide a solid foundation, they were designed using Euclidean datasets and internal validity indices have not been specifically assessed for time series clustering . In contrast to structure-based internal validation, time series clustering algorithms are typically compared by benchmarking them against classification datasets that contain ground truth information. Notable time series benchmarking studies include Javed et al. , which used a phased evaluation framework that isolated the effects of eight algorithms (including partitional, density-based, and hierarchical methods) and three distance functions (Euclidean, dynamic time warping, shapebased) on 112 datasets from the UCR archive . Their analysis found that performance variation depended more on dataset characteristics than algorithmic innovations. Similarly, the Odyssey study from Paparrizos and Reddy  analysed 80 univariate time series clustering methods across 128 datasets. Both studies used external validation indices, since the UCR datasets consist of presegmented univariate time series already assigned to classes. This validation approach, while valuable for evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of algorithms, conflates clustering and classification by assuming presegmented data with known ground truth, which introduces a critical methodological issue of classification boundaries defined by humans that do not necessarily reflect structural properties . Algorithms may perform poorly not because they fail to discover meaningful structures, but because the expected classifications might not match such structures . Additionally to evaluating clustering algorithms for their ability to discover classification labels, these benchmarking studies use real-world datasets. This is both an advantage as such data include the full complexities of time series data but they make it impossible to isolate the performance of the algorithms from the quality of the underlying structures in the data. Our work addresses the gap in correlation-based time series clustering for which distance functions and internal validity indices have not been systematically evaluated. Our perspective is that clustering is a method to find structure in data and therefore the validation techniques need to be based on the quality of the discovered structure not on domain-based labels. 3 Problem Formalisation This section establishes the mathematical formulation and notation of correlation-based clustering and formalises the canonical correlation patterns as discrete clustering validation targets for the infinite correlation space. Throughout, we shall let R denote the set of real numbers and N the set of positive integers. Given a natural number N ∈N, we let [N] := {1, . . . , N}. 3.1 Correlation-based Clustering First, we establish the notation of objects and their relations used in correlation-based clustering. Let X in RT ×V be a matrix where T ∈N is the number of observations and V ∈N is the number of variates in the time series. Given M ∈N we shall let G(M) denote the collection of segmentations into M segments. Formally, for each M ∈N the set G(M) consists of all strictly increasing sequences η = (ηm)M m=0 ∈[T]M+1 of length M +1 with η0 := 0 and ηM := T. For each m ∈[M], the values ηm−1 + 1 and ηm denote the start and end of the m-th index, respectively. We also let G := ST M=1 G(M) denote the set of all possible segmentations of a time horizon T. For each M ∈T, η ∈G(M) and m ∈[M] we let Sm ≡Sm(X, η) := X(ηm−1 + 1, . . . , ηm), (1) which takes values in R|ηm−ηm−1|×V , denote the m-th segment of X, containing sequential observations t ∈{ηm−1 + 1, . . . , ηm}. Then we shall let corr : S R∈N, R≥V RR×V →RV ×V denote the Spearman rank correlation  mapping from R × V matrices ˜X to the corresponding V × V correlation matrix A. The tied values are assigned average ranks, and the Spearman correlation is calculated using the standard tie-corrected formula. For our application of corr, we define the correlation coefficient aij := 0 for the cases of Sm when exactly one of the variates i or j is constant, and aij := 1 when both are constant. The image of corr is contained within the subspace AV ⊆RV ×V consisting of symmetric positive semi-definite matrices with unit diagonal and elements aij ∈[−1, 1] for i, j ∈V and i ̸= j. Note that AV forms a Q-dimensional subspace where Q := V (V −1)/2 is the number of unique pairs of 5 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 variates. As such, we sometimes represent elements of AV by vectors in RQ, where the correlation coefficients aij are ordered lexicographically a U := [a12, a13, ..., a(V −1)V ]. For each segment Sm where m ∈[M], we write Am ≡Am(X, η) := corr(Sm), (2) for its correlation matrix. Next, we write K(M, K) for the set of all clusterings Φ := (ϕ1, . . . , ϕK) which are sequences of K disjoint non-empty subsets of [M] whose union is S Φ = ϕ1 ∪. . . ∪ϕK = [M]. Additionally, we let SC(M, K) denote the set of all segmented clusterings which are tuples of the form π := (η, Φ), (3) where η ∈G(M) and Φ ∈K(M, K) is a clustering of these segments. Furthermore, given π ∈SC(M, K) and m ∈[M] and k ∈[K] we let Ck(π) := {Am : m ∈ϕk}, (4) denote a cluster where ϕk ∈Φ. Finally, to compare how similar two matrices are, we shall leverage a non-negative function d : AV × AV →R≥0 on the space AV as distance function. Given correlation matrices Ax, Ay ∈AV we view d(Ax, Ay) as quantifying the degree of dissimilarity between Ax and Ay. In practice many examples of d will be metrics, yet we require no further properties beyond non-negativity. We provide the definitions for the various distance functions employed in Appendix B. 3.2 Canonical Patterns Next, we formalise the canonical correlation patterns as discrete mathematical validation targets for correlation matrices that underpin our method for correlation-based clustering validation. Let P ∈AV denote a canonical pattern with elements pij ∈{−1, 0, 1} for i, j ∈[V ] and i ̸= j. Each canonical pattern Pℓwith ℓ∈[L] represents a unique idealised correlation structure capturing strong positive correlation, no correlation, or strong negative correlation between the Q unique variate pairs. The total number of different canonical patterns is L := 3Q. A canonical pattern Pℓmust be positive semi-definite to be a valid correlation matrix. To fulfil this requirement, we define a relaxed discretisation criterion where P′ ℓis considered equivalent to its canonical form Pℓ, if P′ ℓis positive semi-definite after adjusting its correlation coefficients within tolerance bands B := {[−1, −0.7], [−0.2, 0.2], [0.7, 1]}. Canonical patterns Pℓthat cannot be made positive semi-definite after this relaxation within B are invalid. The tolerance bands B represent practical thresholds that continue to clearly distinguish between strong negative, negligible, and strong positive correlation coefficients, while respecting the geometry of the correlation space AV . This relaxation process determines which of the L theoretical patterns yield valid correlation matrices, resulting in L′ < L relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓwhere ℓ∈[L′]. To facilitate human interpretation, we use the idealised Pℓto represent a pattern. For calculations, we use the corresponding relaxed form P′ ℓ, see Appendix A for a list of the 23 valid canonical patterns out of the 27 possible and their relaxed form for three time series variates. Let ψ : AV 7→{P′ ℓ: ℓ∈[L′]} denote the canonical pattern mapping ψ(Am) := min argmin ℓ∈[L′] {d(Am, P′ ℓ)} (5) that associates a correlation matrix Am with its closest relaxed canonical pattern. Here, ‘min’ ensures that the ties are broken by selecting the smallest index ℓ. The canonical pattern mapping ψ provides a natural basis for constructing a clustering Φ. A possible clustering strategy is to group correlation matrices in such a way that for k ∈[K] we have ϕk := {m ∈[M] : ψ(Am) = P′ ℓ} , (6) where ℓ∈[L′]. Under such an approach, canonical patterns P′ ℓserve as discrete, idealised, interpretable target clusters of the clustering Φ. Each cluster ϕk then consists of all segment indices m whose correlation matrices map to the same relaxed canonical pattern P′ ℓ. Note that K ≤L′ as not all ℓ∈[L′] need to be present in a given time series X. 6 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 3.3 Level Sets for Canonical Patterns Finally, we introduce level sets that enable a systematic evaluation of distance functions by grouping canonical patterns according to their theoretical similarity. Let d L1 : AV × AV →R≥0 denote the L1 distance between canonical patterns so that d L1(Px, Py) := V X i=1 V X j>i |pxij −pyij|, (7) for pattern indices x, y ∈[L′]. Let DL1 := {δ ∈R : ∃x, y ∈[L′], d L1(Px, Py) = δ} denote the ordered sequence of achievable L1 distances between valid canonical patterns. The theoretical maximum δmax is bounded by V (V −1), although this δmax may not be achievable due to the constraints on valid correlation matrices. To give an example, with three time series variates (V = 3) the sequence becomes DL1 = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, where a distance of 1 represents one coefficient changing by ±1, a distance of 2 represents either two coefficients changing by ±1 or one coefficient flipping sign, and so forth. The theoretical maximum distance of 6 for V = 3 cannot be achieved while only retaining the canonical patterns Pℓthat can satisfy the tolerance bands B and be a valid correlation matrix Am. For each potential distance value δ ∈DL1, we define the level set Lδ as Lδ := {(x, y) : x, y ∈[L′], d L1(Px, Py) = δ}. (8) The collection {Lδ}δ∈DL1 groups pattern index pairs (x, y) by their L1 distance, with L0 containing indices of identical patterns, L1 containing indices of patterns where one correlation coefficient differs by ±1, and so forth. This creates a natural ordering between the level sets, while all the pattern pairs within each Lδ are theoretically equivalent. 4 Evaluation Reference Formulas This section provides established formulas for evaluating the performance of distance functions and assessing clustering quality, providing the mathematical foundation for our methodology. 4.1 Discriminative Power The effectiveness of a distance function d to map empirical correlation matrices Am to their closest canonical patterns P′ ℓ(see Section 3.2) can be evaluated using multiple complementary approaches. We investigate how well a distance function distinguishes across all the canonical patterns, how consistent distances are within a level set Lδ (see Section 3.3) and how well a distance function performs this mapping in the basic 1NN classifier where all the neighbours have been hardcoded to be the canonical patterns. In this section, we provide the established formulas used for these evaluations. 4.1.1 Overall Discriminative Power We use Shannon’s entropy  to evaluate the overall variability of distances. Given a finite number of distances γ ∈D, where D is a multi set, Shannon’s entropy is defined as HD := k X i=1 p(γi) log2(1/p(γi)), (9) where k is the number of bins, γi are the distances falling into bin i, and p(γi) is the relative frequency of the distances in bin i (empirical estimate of the probability mass function for the distances γ ∈D). For the overall discriminative power of a distance function d, we consider all distances. Therefore, D := {γ ∈R≥0 : γ = d(Ax, P′ y)}, where x ∈[M], y ∈[L′], and then |D| = M × L′. The larger HD, the more uncertain and random the observed distances are, which is desirable. 7 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 4.1.2 Level Set Discriminative Power Level sets Lδ (see Section 3.3) lend interpretable properties to evaluate the suitability of a distance function d to map correlation matrices to canonical patterns (see Eq. 5). We expect the distance d between an empirical correlation matrix Am and a canonical pattern P′ ℓto be smaller, the closer the canonical pattern is to the pattern used to create the empirical correlation matrix. We also use Shannon’s entropy to evaluate the similarity of distances within the level sets. For the analysis of the level sets of a distance function d, we consider the subset of distances γ ∈Dδ where Dδ ⊂D for the respective level set Lδ defined as Dδ := {γ ∈R≥0 : γ = d(Ax, P′ y)}, where x ∈[M] and y ∈[L′] such that d L1(Px, Py) = δ, where Px was the canonical pattern used to generate the segment from which the empirical correlation matrix Ax was calculated and Py is the relaxed canonical pattern P′ y we calculate the distance for. The closer to zero HDδ is, the more uniform the observed distances within the level set, which is desirable. The average entropy for all level sets is defined as HL := 1 |DL1| X δ∈DL1 HDδ. (10) Furthermore, the average rate of increase in distances from level set to level set is defined as RL := 1 |DL1| X δ∈DL1 |µLδ −µLδ+1|, (11) where µLδ is the mean distance for the level set Lδ for a distance function. The average rate measures the mean absolute difference in distances between consecutive level sets. 4.1.3 Canonical Pattern Classification Power The ability of a distance function to best map correlation matrices to their matching canonical pattern can be seen as a classification problem. For this we "train" 1NN, the most basic classifier , on the canonical patterns. In this scenario, the neighbours are hardcoded to the canonical patterns. We use this 1NN classifier to assign each empirical correlation matrix to its closest relaxed canonical pattern using a distance function d. Since each class is equally as important, we calculate the macro F1 score to assess how well a distance function performs at this task; see Appendix C for the exact definition. 4.2 Clustering Quality The quality of a segmented clustering (often referred to as partition of a dataset in the literature) πi ∈SC(M, K) (see Eq. 3) is commonly assessed using external and/or internal validity indices . 4.2.1 External Validity Index External validation of a segmented clustering πi is only possible when a ground truth partition πG is known. Our aim is to identify both distance functions that can discriminate between the different canonical correlation patterns and map empirical correlation matrices to their canonical patterns, as well as internal validity indices that quantify the quality of a particular segmented clustering. The distance functions and internal indices selected must provide good interpretability, computational stability, and robustness to common variations in the quality of real-life data. For both evaluations, we follow a systematic three-stage methodology in which we first select candidates; second empirically evaluate their performance; and third, statistically validate whether there are superior options. We recognise that statistically significant differences may not always translate to meaningful practical improvements and therefore evaluate both practical and statistical differences between candidates. Importantly, we assess distance function performance in two distinct contexts. First, we evaluate their ability to directly discriminate between canonical correlation patterns. Second, we evaluate how these same distance functions perform when embedded within internal validity indices for clustering quality assessment. As we demonstrate, optimal distance functions may differ between these contexts. For statistical testing, we employ a two-phase approach (exploratory and confirmatory) to reduce false discoveries, organising the tests into six families to control Type I error rates . We conduct the experiments using the CSTS benchmark datasets , which provides validated ground truth clusterings for all canonical patterns under normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified data conditions. CSTS further provides controlled degraded quality clustering as well as reduced cluster and segment count versions to enable a thorough investigation of the effectiveness and potential biases of the validation methods. 5.1 Canonical Pattern Mapping Assessment Our aim in this section is to identify which distance functions best map empirical correlation matrices to their underlying canonical patterns. We describe how we select candidate distance functions and then evaluate their ability to distinguish between different canonical correlation patterns, as well as validate whether there is a superior distance function. 5.1.1 Distance Function Selection We select distance functions using the following four key principles: 1. Interpretability: The distance function must follow human intuition about similarity and differences between correlation matrices Am and canonical patterns Pℓ. The distance function should allow meaningful interpretations of which cluster Ck(π) best fits each observed correlation matrix Am and which cluster best fits a canonical pattern Pℓ. 2. Discriminative Power: The distance function must be able to effectively and reliably distinguish between the different canonical patterns Pℓand assign correlation matrices Am to their closest canonical pattern Pℓ, see the canonical pattern mapping equation 5. Each canonical pattern should be equally distinguishable. 3. Computational Stability: The distance function must be numerically stable. This includes dealing with very small eigenvalues λi and singular correlation matrices, which are both common in the relaxed canonical patterns P′ ℓ. The computation time needs to be feasible on standard hardware, prioritising result quality over processing speed. 4. Robustness: The distance function needs to be able to handle real-world challenges such as varying segment lengths, irregular sampling, and non-normal distributions of the time series variates without the need for manual parameter tuning, which is not possible without knowing the ground truth. Following these four principles, we select the vector-based distance functions Lp norm, Lp norm with reference vector, dot transformed Lp norm, and the matrix-based distance functions Log Frobenius norm and Förstner metric (all defined in Appendix B). We focus on vector-based distance functions 11 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 because of their direct quantification of the differences in correlation coefficients and easy geometrical interpretation. We include matrix-based distance functions because they, to varying degrees, capture the geometry of correlation matrices, which could be advantageous. Our selection includes distance functions that are directly applicable to correlation matrices without requiring parameter tuning. This excludes time series specific distance function like Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), which requires parameter tuning and measures distance between time series observations rather than correlations. We also focus on distance functions with direct geometric interpretation for correlation matrices, excluding probabilistic and graph-based approaches. 5.1.2 Distance Function Evaluation We systematically evaluate the performance of the selected distance functions to identify which dissimilarity function best satisfies our four key principles to map empirical correlation matrices to canonical patterns. Each distance function is assessed against criteria derived from the principles of interpretability and discriminative power, with robustness and computational stability serving as a prerequisite for inclusion; see details in Section 6.2. For interpretability, we evaluate whether distance functions produce intuitive mappings between empirical correlation matrices and canonical patterns. This includes evaluating distance consistency within level sets (see Eq. 8) and meaningful separation between level sets. For discriminative power, we assess each distance function’s ability to reliably distinguish between canonical patterns and correctly assign empirical correlation matrices to their closest canonical pattern. This evaluation focusses on the distance function’s capacity to maintain clear boundaries between different canonical patterns and accurately assign empirical correlation matrices. We rank distance functions based on their performance for each of these criteria, providing both relative comparisons between distance functions and overall performance evaluation to ensure that high-ranking distance functions demonstrate genuine effectiveness rather than merely superior relative performance. The evaluation is carried out separately for normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified data conditions to assess robustness and identify distance functions that maintain consistent performance under real-world challenges. 5.1.3 Statistical Validation To statistically validate whether the distance function ranked highest is superior, we use Wilcoxon signed rank tests  to compare the distance function ranks for each subject. These tests constitute Family 1 of our six-family statistical testing framework, specifically designed to control Type I error rates when determining which distance functions best map correlation matrices to canonical patterns. In the exploratory phase, we employ a step-down procedure starting with the two best-ranked distance functions and expanding comparisons until significant differences are found. We allow for different distance functions to achieve significantly lower ranks for different data variants. Based on exploratory findings, we preregister the directional hypotheses for confirmatory tests , see Table 1. 5.2 Internal Validity Index Assessment Having established optimal distance functions for canonical pattern discrimination, we now aim to identify which distance functions optimise the performance of the internal validity index and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable quantification of clustering quality with minimal bias. We first describe how we select candidate internal clustering validity indices and then evaluate using different distance functions their ability to reliably quantify the quality of a segmented clustering (see Equation 3), as well as validate whether there is a superior distance function and internal index combination. 5.2.1 Index Selection We select the internal validity indices to evaluate based on their performance in previous comprehensive evaluation studies by Vendramin et al.  and Arbelaitz et al.  as well as based on their popularity in clustering. Due to our canonical pattern approach of defining an upper bound for the possible number of patterns in a dataset, it is important that the number of clusters K and the number 12 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 of segments M do not affect the performance of the internal validity index, as not every canonical pattern will be present in every dataset despite the clustering being of equal high quality. 5.2.2 Index Evaluation We evaluate the selected internal indices to determine which distance functions optimise internal validity index performance and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable clustering quality assessment with minimal bias. We systematically evaluate both objectives for each data variant to understand how the choice of distance function affects index performance and how different indices behave under varying conditions. We evaluate how different distance functions affect internal validity index performance from two complementary perspectives. First, we assess each distance function’s ability to produce optimal raw index values for the highest-quality segmented clustering (ground-truth perfect clustering). Second, we evaluate how well each distance function enables indices to correlate with the Jaccard index, measuring the index’s ability to distinguish between different clustering quality levels. The latter perspective shows how validation without labels (internal clustering validation) matches validation using ground truth label information (external clustering validation, not available in real-world settings). We independently assess these two perspectives for each data variant and internal validity index, then synthesise the results to identify optimal distance functions. When optimal distance functions differ between raw performance and correlation performance, we examine the implications of this divergence from a practical viewpoint. Using the optimal distance functions identified above, we assess the reliability and bias of the internal validity indices. We evaluate the sensitivity of the index to varying numbers of clusters and segments by working with reduced versions of our data variants. Additionally, we synthesise results across all data variants (normal, non-normal, downsampled, and sparsified) to assess the robustness of each index to different data characteristics and pattern degradation conditions. 5.2.3 Statistical Validation To statistically validate whether there is a superior distance function for the validity indices and an overall superior validity index, we use Wilcoxon signed rank tests to compare the evaluation results for each subject . These tests constitute Families 2-6 of our six-family statistical testing framework. We first establish which distance function and internal index combinations achieve sufficient correlation strength to warrant detailed comparative analysis. We apply a viability threshold that requires Pearson’s mean correlation |r| > 0.5 between the internal indices and the Jaccard index for each subject within each data variant, based on sample size calculations to ensure adequate statistical power. Based on viable combinations from this filtering, we define the five families (2-6) comparing the internal indices SWC and DBI, which pass this correlation viability threshold. Family 2 evaluates which distance function achieves significantly better ground truth values for SWC and DBI, while Family 3 evaluates which distance function achieves significantly stronger correlation between SWC/DBI and the Jaccard index. Family 4 examines whether SWC or DBI correlates more strongly with the Jaccard index, Family 5 examines the impacts of cluster count reduction, and Family 6 evaluates the effects of segment count reduction. In the exploratory phase, we employ a step-down procedure starting with the two best performing distance functions and internal indices, respectively, expanding comparisons until significant differences are found. We allow for different distance functions and internal indices to achieve significantly lower ranks for different data variants. Based on these exploratory findings, we preregister the directional hypotheses for confirmatory tests using hierarchical testing procedures , see Tables 2 to 6. 6 Experimental Setup We describe the experimental setup in four parts. First, we describe the CSTS benchmark dataset used for all experiments. Second, we present the experimental configurations for the canonical pattern mapping assessment following our three-stage methodology: candidate selection, evaluation implementation, and statistical validation. Third, we detail the experimental configurations for the 13 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 internal validity index assessment, following the same three-stage structure. The Jaccard index linearly increases as the number of wrongly assigned clusters decreases from all 100 segments having a wrong cluster assigned to none (first 44 segmented clusterings). It continues to increase, all be it at a slower rate, as the number of observation shifted decreases (last 22 segmented clustering). Simply shifting observation has less of an impact on the Jaccard index than assigning a segment to a wrong cluster. 6.3.1 Index Selection Following the method defined in Section 5.2, we selected the following four internal indices: (1) the silhouette width criterion (SWC; see Eq. 17) for its consistent high performance and lack of needing a cluster or data centroid; (2) the relatively little known Pakhira-Bandyopadhyay-Maulik index (PBM, see Eq. 20) due to its good performance in  and its robustness to varying numbers of clusters; (3) the widely used Davies-Bouldin index (DBI, see Eq. 18); and (4) the Calinksi-Harabasz index (VRC, see Eq. 19). The latter two were chosen for their popularity in clustering quality assessments. 6.3.2 Index Evaluation To evaluate which distance functions optimise internal validity index performance and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable clustering quality quantification, we performed assessments on all data variants, each containing the same ND = 30 subjects. To identify optimal distance functions for internal validity indices, we first calculated all four internal validity indices (SWC, PBM, DBI, VRC) for the ground truth segmented clusterings using ten representative distance functions selected based on the canonical pattern mapping assessment. These distance functions span the Lp distance family (L1, L2, L3, L5, Linf), referenceand dot-transformbased variants (L1 ref, L5 ref, dt Linf) and correlation-specialised approaches (Log Frobenius, Förstner). We ranked distance functions based on their ability to produce optimal raw index values for ground truth clusterings. Second, we calculated Pearson correlations between internal indices and the Jaccard index for each distance function on clusterings of degraded quality that span the full 17 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 range of the Jaccard index . Note that evaluating segmentation and clustering of time series simultaneously is uncommon, which required our adapted Jaccard index definition (see Eq. 14) for segmented clusterings. To reduce the number of combinations to evaluate and achieve statistically significant correlations, we established that all internal indices had to achieve a minimum correlation strength of |r| ≥0.5 (see Section 6.3.3) for at least one distance function, which only SWC and DBI did. VRC and PBM showed insufficient correlations with the Jaccard index, with correlations reaching at best 0.21−0.48. Consequently, VRC and PBM were excluded from a detailed comparative analysis. We focused the detailed raw value analysis on SWC and DBI, calculating 95% confidence intervals of the mean ground truth index values across subjects of the ten aforementioned distance functions. The correlation analysis aligns with the study setup in . To assess index reliability and bias, we recalculated all internal indices for the reduced versions of the correlated and non-normal data variants with 50% and 25% of the original clusters (11 and 6 patterns, respectively) and segments (50 and 25 segments, respectively). For this analysis, we use the L5 distance function based on its consistent performance in achieving optimal index values across data variants. For computational stability, we addressed division-by-zero cases in the DBI index by introducing a minimal cluster centroid distance of dmin(ACk, ACy) = 10−15 when identical centroids occurred. For data variants that produce constant index values (raw), we set the correlation coefficients to 0 and p-values to 1 to enable batch processing while indicating the absence of correlation. 6.3.3 Statistical Validation For viable correlation strength filtering, we calculated sample size requirements using equation  Nπ = b + c2( zα + z1−β z(ρ1) −z(ρ0))2, (24) with b = 3 and c2 = 1, ρ0 = 0.5, ρ1 = 0.7, α = 0.05, and β = 0.8. z(•) denotes the Fisher transform and zα = 1.645 respectively z1−β = 0.84 denote the Gaussian critical values for α respectively 1 −β. The required sample size was ≥65 degraded clusterings per subject. With 67 clusterings available, combinations that achieve Pearson’s |r| ≥0.5 between an internal index and the Jaccard index demonstrate statistical significance with power ≥80%. For each data variant with correlation patterns (excluding raw variants), we calculated Wilcoxon signed rank tests with ND = 30 subjects. The exploratory analysis used two-sided tests with α = 0.05 to identify promising patterns. Based on these findings, we preregistered the confirmatory hypotheses listed in Tables 1 through 6. We organised the confirmatory analysis into five families, each addressing specific aspects of internal index performance. For Family 2, which compares how well different distance functions produce optimal internal validity indices for the ground truth segmented clustering for SWC and DBI, we excluded pairs with differences < 0.0001 and used Sci Py’s exact p-value implementation. For SWC higher values indicate better clustering quality, while for DBI values lower values indicate better quality. They hypotheses reflect this. For Family 3 correlation strength comparisons, we calculated Pearson’s correlation coefficients between internal indices and the Jaccard index for each distance function, excluding pairs with correlation differences < 0.001. Since DBI exhibits negative correlation with the Jaccard index, while SWC shows positive correlation, we multiplied the correlation coefficients of DBI by −1 to allow comparison of the correlation strengths. For Family 4, which compares the correlation strength between SWC and DBI, we selected the distance function L5 based on exploratory analysis showing balanced performance across both indices and data variants. L5 achieved best-ranked or non-significantly different from best-ranked for both SWC and DBI across multiple conditions, ensuring that neither index is systematically disadvantaged in the comparative analysis. We excluded pairs with differences < 0.001. Since DBI exhibits negative correlation with the Jaccard index, while SWC shows positive correlation, we multiplied the correlation coefficients of DBI by −1 to allow comparison of the correlation strengths. For Families 5 and 6 that examine the effects of the cluster and segment count on the ground truth values for SWC, respectively, DBI, we used the L5 distance function for consistency with the Family 4 comparisons and excluded pairs with differences < 0.0001. DBI50 > DBI25 1.02 29 7 Results Given the extensive experiments conducted across multiple distance functions, internal validity indices, and data variants, it would be overwhelming to report all results in full. Instead, we focus on findings that directly provide answers to which distance functions best map empirical correlation matrices to canonical patterns and which internal indices best assess clustering quality. For reporting results for the 9 different data variants (normal, non-normal, downsampled, each with the three sparsity levels complete - 100%, partial - 70%, and sparse - 10%), we establish the normal, complete data variant as our baseline that represents ideal conditions researchers typically assume. For each major finding, we first report this baseline performance and then describe important deviations for the other variants instead of exhaustively listing all combinations. 7.1 Canonical Pattern Mapping Assessment Here we present the results determining which distance functions best map correlation matrices to canonical patterns through direct discrimination. Overall, we showed that L1-based distance functions consistently achieved superior performance for canonical pattern mapping across data variants. 7.1.1 Distance Function Evaluation For our baseline, the normal and complete data variant, the L1 norm distance function ranked best (µ = 4.7, SD= 0.07), followed by L3 (µ = 4.76, 0.15) and L1 ref (µ = 4.82, 0.12), while the Förstner level ranked worst (µ = 6.57, 0.10). See Figure 4a for a heat map of the average rank of the 15 distance functions across data variants. For the non-normal variants, L1 ref was top ranked (µ = 4.52, 0.2) and L1 moved to second best rank (µ = 4.71, 0.1), for the downsampled variants the L1 norm stayed best ranked (µ = 3.64, 0.27) but second best was the L2 (µ = 4.31, 0.37) norm. The ranking order of the distance functions was generally not affected by sparsity other than sometimes for the sparse variant. Evaluating criterion-specific differences show that L1’s overall superiority reflected strong discriminative power performance that compensated for moderate interpretability scores, while the specialised distance functions such as Förstner and Log Frobenius excelled in narrow domains but failed to achieve balanced performance across both evaluation principles. No single distance function achieved 21 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 (a) average ranks (b) criterion-level raw values Figure 4: Distance function performance for pattern mapping across data variants: (a) average rank for the 15 distance functions (b) raw criterion values for top-ranked L1 and L1 ref. Highlighted cells show best performers; darker colours indicate better performance. consistent superiority. For interpretability, Linf and dt Linf excelled in maintaining distances close to zero for level set zero (criterion 1: µ = 1, SD= 0), while L1 performed moderately (µ = 5.2, SD= 0.41) and Förstner ranked worst (µ = 13.2, SD= 0.41). All Lp norm-based distance functions achieved perfect performance in ensuring significant and monotonically increasing differences between level sets (criterion 2: µ = 1, SD= 0), separating them from Förstner and Log Frobenius (µ = 2.0, SD= 0). However, for the rate of increase between level sets (criterion 3), Log Frobenius ranked best (µ = 1, SD= 0), L1 fell to middle performance (µ = 8, SD= 0), and Linf ranked worst (µ = 14, SD= 0). For discriminative power, L1 ref dominated overall entropy maximisation (criterion 4: µ = 1, SD= 0) while L1 performed poorly (µ = 12, SD= 0), but this pattern reversed for level set entropy minimisation (criterion 5) where L1 ranked best (µ = 1, SD= 0) and L3 ref worst (µ = 13.9, SD= 0.64). The macro F1 classification criterion (6) again favoured all distance functions based on the Lp norm (µ = 1, SD= 0), with Log Frobenius (µ = 12, SD= 0) and Förstner (µ = 3, SD= 0) trailing significantly. For the non-normal and complete data variant, L1 ref achieved overall superiority (µ = 4.5 vs. L1 µ = 4.7) primarily through markedly improved performance on the rate of increase between level sets (criterion 3: L1 ref improved from µ = 3.0 to µ = 1.87 while L1 remained at µ = 8.0) and modest improvement in level set entropy minimisation (criterion 5: µ = 11.73 to µ = 10.78), while L1 changed minimally. For all other criteria, the differences between normal and non-normal variants were minimal for both distance functions. For downsampled variants, we compared to non-normal rather than normal data since downsampled data remains non-normally distributed . Although we therefore expected L1 ref to maintain superiority for downsampled data variants, L1 regained overall superiority (µ = 3.7 vs. L1 ref µ = 6.8) through a dramatic role reversal on entropy maximisation (criterion 4: L1 improved from µ = 11.9 (SD=0.25) to µ = 1.17 (SD=0.38) while L1 ref deteriorated from µ = 1.1 (SD=0.31) to µ = 9.17 (SD=0.67) and superior resilience to classification degradation (criterion 6: L1 µ = 2.67, SD=1.52 vs. L1 ref µ = 6.23, SD=2.25), as perfect classification performance was no longer achievable under downsampled conditions. For the classification criterion, L1, L2, and L3 were the only distance functions that remained ranked < 3. While L1 ref maintained its advantage on the rate of increase between level sets (criterion 3: µ = 1.8, SD=0.81 vs. L1 µ = 6.0, SD=0), L1’s gains on criteria 4 and 6 outweighed this, with L1 ref’s substantial deterioration on multiple criteria explaining its overall ranking decline. Figure 4b shows the raw criterion values for the top performing distance functions L1 (normal and downsampled data variants) and L1 ref (non-normal data variants) across all data variants, illustrating how L1 ref achieves superior maximisation of entropy (criterion 4: 4.3 vs 1.6 for normal data) while L1 dominates minimisation of entropy (criterion 5: 1.6 vs 2.9), with both distance functions maintaining near perfect classification performance with F1 (criterion 6: 1.0) except under downsampled conditions where performance slightly degrades (0.93 −0.96). 22 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 For background on the differences observed in downsampled variants, it is important to note that downsampling non-normal data from 1 sec to 1 min distorts correlation patterns . 7.1.2 Statistical Validation Confirmatory statistical validation tests of the preregister hypotheses (see Table 1) in a hierarchical procedure confirmed the superiority of L1 over L1 ref for the normal data variants, L1 ref over L1 for the non-normal data variants, and L1 over L2 for downsampled data variants. All tests achieved statistical significance , with consistently large effect sizes (0.69 −1.1) and high statistical power (≥97%), see Table E.1 for detailed results. The effect sizes were the smallest for the normal variants (0.93) and non-normal sparse variants (0.69). This was not the case for the sparse and downsampled variant (1.1). 7.2 Internal Validity Index Assessment Here we present results determining which distance functions optimise internal validity index performance and which internal validity indices provide the most reliable clustering quality assessment with minimal bias. Overall, we show that L5 emerged as the optimal distance function for internal validity indices, while both SWC and DBI showed systematic bias patterns and both provide different insights into evaluating clustering quality. 7.2.1 Index Evaluation For our baseline normal and complete data variant, the distance functions L3, L5, Linf, and dt Linf all lead to the same highest SWC values (µ = 0.98, SD=0.0) for the ground truth clustering, while for DBI these same distance functions and additionally L2, and L5 ref resulted in the same best ground truth performance (lowest values, µ = 0.04, SD=0.01). For the complete and non-normal data variant, these same distance functions maintained optimal performance for both indices, with SWC and DBI values remaining virtually unchanged. However, the performance of the downsampled data variant for all distance functions was degraded, with SWC values dropping to approximately µ = 0.62, (SD=0.05) and DBI values increasing to around µ = 0.5 (SD=0.07). The relative ranking of the distance functions remained consistent. Progressive sparsification from complete (100%) to partial (70%) to sparse (10%) data variants showed a gradual slight performance degradation for normal and non-normal data variants, with SWC decreasing from 0.98 (SD=0) to 0.97 (SD=0) to 0.92 (SD=0.01) and DBI increasing from 0.04 (SD=0.01) to 0.05 (SD=0.01) to 0.14 (SD=0.02) for the optimal distance functions, while maintaining the same relative performance hierarchy across all sparsification levels. For the downsampled data variants, the best performance was observed for the sparse (SWC= 0.67, DBI=0.44), second best for the partial (SWC= 0.63, DBI=0.49) and worst for the complete data variant (SWC= 0.62, DBI=0.5). First, we synthesise the primary results for distance function performance in canonical pattern mapping and internal validity index optimisation for correlationbased clustering. Second, we compare our findings with previous clustering validation studies, highlighting how our method differs by focusing on the ability of internal indices to assess structural quality rather than identifying the optimal number of clusters or achieving the strongest correlation with external indices. Third, we provide practical recommendations for implementing correlationbased clustering validation in applied research contexts, including concrete index value thresholds that indicate the presence of strong correlation patterns similar to canonical patterns. Finally, we acknowledge the limitations of our approach and outline directions for future research. 8.1 Primary Results Our results reveal that simple, interpretable Lp norm distances outperform more complex and specialised distance functions for correlation-based clustering validation. Although optimal choices vary statistically between data variants, practical differences are often minimal. This allows simplified recommendations for practitioners, such as using the L1 norm distance function to map correlation matrices to canonical patterns, and the L5 norm distance function to calculate the silhouette width criterion (SWC) and the Davies-Bouldin index (DBI), which both evaluate correlation-based clusterings well; see Section 4 for clustering quality index definitions. Canonical pattern mapping was practically optimised by the L1 norm, which excelled at discriminative power while maintaining interpretability. Statistically, the L1 norm was the best for normal and downsampled data variants , while the L1 ref emerged as significantly better for non-normal data variants . However, despite these statistically robust differences that affect average ranks, the magnitude of differences in raw criterion values was so small that rounding masked them. Therefore, practically speaking, the choice between L1 and L1 ref is unlikely to substantially impact canonical pattern mapping performance. Sparsification made distance functions perform less well without impacting which distance function performed best. Surprisingly, the more sophisticated correlation-specific distance functions Förstner and Log Frobenius consistently ranked in the bottom third. Internal validity index optimisation revealed different optimal performing distance functions than for canonical pattern mapping. Practically, the L5 norm provided the most robust choice across data variants for both SWC and DBI. Statistically, the optimal distance function varied between conditions. L5 significantly outperformed L3 for SWC in normal data , while patterns reversed for downsampled variants where Linf outperformed L5 . Similarly, for DBI, L5 ref significantly outperformed L3 across normal and non-normal variants , while L5 outperformed L3 in 27 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 Figure 8: Scatter plots for internal validity indices (green, x, right y-axes) compared to the Jaccard index (pink, o, left y-axes) of the 67 segmented clusterings of various quality for 30 subjects. This is the data for the non-normal, partial (70%) variant. The distance function used to calculate the internal indices was the L5 norm. downsampled and Linf in normal and non-normal sparse conditions . However, the confidence intervals show (see Figure 5) that the practical differences between the Lp norms were minimal, suggesting that any of these distance functions would produce comparable results. Again, sophisticated correlation-specific distance functions performed poorly and should be avoided. When evaluating the correlation strength with the Jaccard index, both SWC and DBI achieved strong correlations (|r| > 0.9), while the Calinski-Harabasz index (VRC) and the Pakhira-Bandyopadhyay-Maulik index (PBM) failed to meet the minimal requirements (|r| > 0.5) for all the selected distance functions. Segment count sensitivity analysis revealed important practical limitations. SWC degrades significantly when clusters contain fewer than two objects, dropping from 0.92 (100 segments) to 0.88 (50 segments) to 0.59 (25 segments), while DBI paradoxically showed improved performance (0.04 to 0.037 to 0.025). This indicates that SWC requires more than two objects per cluster to be able to assess within-cluster similarity, while DBI improves with smaller clusters. These effects are both statistically and practically significant, as shown in the confidence intervals in Figure 7. Cluster count sensitivity analysis showed that both indices favoured lower cluster counts, with significant improvements when reducing from 23 to 6 clusters (p<0.001-0.033). However, practically, the bias towards fewer clusters is unlikely to affect clustering validation, with SWC improving marginally from 0.92 to 0.93 and DBI from 0.1 to 0.14. Index reliability comparison revealed that both SWC and DBI provide reliable correlation-based clustering validation with strong correlations to the Jaccard index and differentiated well between clustering quality levels. SWC demonstrated stricter evaluation of segmentation errors compared to DBI, which may be advantageous depending on application requirements. Both indices significantly outperformed VRC and PBM, whose values for perfect clustering results spanned several orders of magnitude , making reliable interpretation impractical; see Figure 8. 8.2 Comparison with Previous Work Previous clustering validation studies (see Section 2) focus on identifying the ’right’ number of clusters (defined by human categories) rather than assessing the structural quality of the clustering results. This fundamental difference in validation philosophy leads to different conclusions about index performance and creates a gap in providing practitioners with structural quality guidelines. Our approach differs by validating the performance of indices directly on synthetically created cluster assignments with verified correlation structures, rather than by validating clustering algorithm results. This isolated the ability of indices to discover structures from the ability of clustering algorithms to recover those structures, enabling precise quantification of each index’s structure discovery ability and response to different real-world data conditions (distribution shifts, downsampling, sparsification) as well as potential sensitivity towards reduced number of clusters and objects. Furthermore, these perturbations were applied to the same 60 datasets (we call them subjects), creating versions of the same subject for different conditions. This is unlike previous studies in which such factors have been investigated by analysing entirely different datasets, which does not avoid introducing variations that affect indices beyond the particular perturbation being studied . Above all, the structures we studied were correlation structures, not Euclidean points, for which we introduced the framework of canonical patterns that provides discrete known target correlation structures that 28 Preprint: Validating Clustering Validation - July 23, 2025 serve a similar purpose, like geometrical shapes in the Euclidean space. Most importantly, our design of the canonical patterns leads to a limited number of possible patterns, transforming the clustering challenge from finding the elusive right number of clusters to discovering which of the known canonical patterns exist in a particular dataset. Although SWC consistently ranks among the strongest indices across studies , our work uniquely demonstrates that DBI performs comparably well for correlation-based clustering. This contrasts with previous Euclidean studies in which DBI typically underperformed relative to VRC and PBM. In contrast, VRC and PBM, which showed strong performance in geometric clustering contexts, failed to reliably detect our ground truth and struggled to differentiate between segmented clusterings with controlled degraded quality. This divergence likely stems from a combination of our focus on reliable threshold values for structure-based ground truth versus the usual focus on optimal value for the ’right’ number of clusters, as well as how the indices are designed to assess within-cluster cohesion and between-cluster separation. Both VRC and PBM rely on geometric concepts such as overall dataset centroid, which translate poorly to the correlation space. In contrast, DBI only uses cluster centroids, whereas SWC relies solely on object-to-object dissimilarity assessments that remain meaningful across object types. In addition, we identified segment count (object count) sensitivity as a previously undocumented factor that affects internal indices. When reducing the segment count per cluster from 4-5 to 0-2, SWC degrades significantly, while DBI shows improved performance. This phenomenon highlights SWC emphasis on assessing both within-cluster similarity (which suffers with fewer objects) and inter-cluster separation. We selected studies that published index values and used datasets that have their structures at least visualised.
